item.content:encoded:
Newly released records detail synchronized drone formations, reported radio interference affecting military personnel, and FBI involvement in investigations that failed to identify the operators.

Nearly two years after unauthorized drone activity prompted the closure of the airfield at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (WPAFB) in Ohio, newly released investigative records reveal additional details about the December 2024 incidents, including reports of synchronized drone maneuvers and communications disruptions experienced by military personnel.

The documents, released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on November 13, 2026, and received by The Black Vault on November 25, originated with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). They detail three separate periods of reported drone activity between December 11 and 17, 2024, two of which were designated as FBI-led investigative matters.

All three AFOSI investigative communications are marked closed. In each instance, the operators of the aircraft remained unidentified.

The records were obtained only after The Black Vault challenged AFOSI’s initial determination that it had no responsive records concerning the incidents.

From “No Records” to an FBI Referral

Under Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request 2025-06621-F, The Black Vault sought AFOSI investigative reports, intelligence assessments, threat evaluations and interagency correspondence concerning the December 2024 drone incursions.

In July 2025, AFOSI issued a “no records” response.

That determination was challenged on July 16, 2025, through an administrative appeal citing previously released Air Force documents that explicitly documented AFOSI’s notification of the incidents.

On January 6, 2026, AFOSI issued its final response to the appeal. Rather than maintaining its original determination, the agency acknowledged that responsive records had been referred to the FBI.

“All the records responsive to your request have been referred to another federal agency, FBI,” wrote Roxanne M. Jensen, Chief of AFOSI’s Information Release Branch.

When The Black Vault requested clarification regarding the original determination, AFOSI Information Release Specialist John Jordan responded on January 7:

“You are correct, you did receive a ‘no records’ response. Eventually we received the record in our database and processed it.”

The explanation raises questions about how AFOSI maintained and processed investigative information concerning the incursions.

All three investigative communications ultimately released carry a transmittal date of September 8, 2025, nearly nine months after the incidents and less than two months after The Black Vault filed its appeal.

While those dates do not establish that the specific documents existed at the time of the original FOIA search, the communications themselves document AFOSI’s involvement in December 2024, including interviews conducted jointly with the FBI.

Where that underlying investigative information was maintained before it entered the database, and why it was not located during the original search, remain unanswered.

The FBI ultimately reviewed and released seven pages under FOIPA request 1708151-000, with redactions that the FBI specifically attributed to AFOSI.

Drone Activity Began Before the Airfield Closure

The first of the three investigative communications documents drone activity on the night of December 11, 2024, continuing into the following morning — two days before the incidents that prompted the airfield closure.

Security Forces personnel reported observing an unmanned aircraft hovering over the installation’s military working dog kennel. Searches for suspicious personnel or packages yielded negative results.

Initial reports described an aircraft approximately five by six feet in size and operating with four rotors.

According to AFOSI:

“Interview of SFS personnel disclosed that the sUAS displayed steady and flashing red, white, and green lights, and they did not see visible cameras or payloads on the sUAS.”

Air Force Materiel Command reported that it was not tracking anything in the area and had no scheduled drone events. FAA offices in Columbus and Cincinnati also reported being unaware of drone flights matching the description.

The matter was designated as FBI-led. The investigative communication concludes:

“The operator(s) of the sUAS was not identified.”

Military Personnel Reported Radio Disruptions During Drone Encounters

Among the most significant revelations in the new release are details obtained during joint FBI and AFOSI interviews with Security Forces personnel on December 14, 2024.

One witness described observing a drone approximately one to two feet in length, traveling between 30 and 40 miles per hour. After illuminating the aircraft with a spotlight, the witness described a “dark gray clover-shaped body, with four propellers housed by black protectors.”

The witness also reported seeing the aircraft perform a vertical loop, as if it was “performing tricks.”

The same individual subsequently observed four drones flying in a diamond formation, separated by approximately one foot. When illuminated by a spotlight, the aircraft reportedly extinguished their lights, simultaneously banked to the right, accelerated and gained altitude before departing.

However, the investigative communication documents another detail concerning the encounters: the reported disruption of military communications equipment.

According to AFOSI:

“The 88 SFS member stated that during both sightings, they were approximately 80 feet from the sUAS, and while the sUAS were near, they were not able to utilize their radio, in that they were not able to send a signal and the only sound from the radio was muffled and distorted.”

The document continues:

“The 88 SFS member’s partner also experienced the same radio issues. After the sUASs departed, their radios functioned properly.”

The released records contain no technical assessment explaining the reported communications disruption. Whether investigators examined the radios, conducted radio-frequency analysis or considered the possibility of deliberate electronic interference is unknown.

The account establishes a reported correlation between the presence of the drones and the communications problems, but it does not establish causation.

Investigators Determined One Sighting Was Mistaken

The newly released records also reveal that investigators determined at least one reported drone sighting during the December 13 incident was erroneous.

AFOSI documented the finding following interviews with Security Forces personnel:

“However, upon further investigation, it was identified that the member was mistaken and a sUAS was not viewed.”

The document does not explain what the individual actually observed, what evidence investigators used to reach that determination, or whether similar assessments were conducted for other reported sightings.

Despite that finding, the same investigative communication documents the separate observations of synchronized drone formations and attributes the airfield closure to the reported drone activity.

The operators were never identified in the released investigative summary.

AFOSI Personnel Witnessed Drones; Thermal Imaging Also Used

The third investigative communication, concerning the December 16–17 incidents, establishes that AFOSI personnel were not solely relying on observations reported by other military personnel.

According to the document:

“At 2237 hours, OSI 10 FIS reported visually observing at least 6 sUAS loitering over Area A, WPAFB, OH.”

The records also reveal that Wright-Patterson Fire Department personnel reported observing four drones using thermal imaging equipment. One of those aircraft was reported in the general vicinity of the National Air and Space Intelligence Center (NASIC).

Additional observations by Security Forces personnel included drones hovering above the National Museum of the United States Air Force and two drones flying over NASIC.

No thermal imagery is included in the FBI release. Whether the equipment recorded the observations, whether any recordings were preserved, and whether investigators subsequently analyzed that material remain unknown.

The document also contains a discrepancy involving local law enforcement. AFOSI recorded a notification from Dayton Metro Parks Police that its patrols had observed a drone flying toward the installation. Later in the same investigative communication, AFOSI states that coordination with Metro Parks Police yielded reports that none of its patrols had observed drone activity.

Investigators Examined Video of a Suspected Unmanned Aircraft

The newly released documents also confirm that investigators obtained video evidence of an aircraft previously described in sworn military witness statements obtained by The Black Vault.

During the December 16 incident, multiple Security Forces personnel reported observing an airplane conducting a low approach over the Wright-Patterson runway before climbing away.

AFOSI documented the existence of a recording:

“88 SFS members provided a 16 second video of the suspected sUAS which showed an object in the sky illuminated with what appeared to be red and green wingtips, and a red flashing beacon light similar to one on an aircraft indicating the engines are on.”

As previously reported by The Black Vault, one Security Forces witness described the aircraft as gray, possessing wings and engines, and estimated it to be larger than an F-16.

The newly released investigative communication does not establish whether investigators ultimately identified the aircraft as manned or unmanned.

It also states that Wright-Patterson Airfield Management Operations and Air Traffic Control reported not seeing any aircraft or drones in the airspace during the incident. Airfield Management Operations clarified that its shift began at approximately 11 p.m.

That account is particularly noteworthy given previously released FAA records documenting between seven and 17 radar targets during the same evening. Although tower personnel reported no visual observations, the FAA records document that Security Forces personnel on the ground reportedly identified the activity as drones.

Whether investigators correlated the video, eyewitness observations and radar returns is not addressed in the new release.

The 16-second video itself was not included in this release, but may be one of those released previously (that are close to 16 seconds) here.

Investigators Pursued Leads Involving Vehicles Near the Base

The new records also provide details about investigative efforts to identify potential drone operators outside the installation.

Wright-Patterson Fire Department personnel reported observing a vehicle parked off the installation while using thermal imaging equipment. The vehicle was facing the airfield, although the quality of the imagery prevented personnel from determining its exact make and model.

The investigative communication documents a review of Flock Safety camera footage in connection with the vehicle observation.

A subsequent entry dated December 18 documents investigative efforts concerning a vehicle reported parked off-base near the airfield.

Investigators used the Flock Safety system to obtain information and conducted interviews.

The registered owner acknowledged owning a small hobby drone approximately six to eight inches in size but reported being unaware of drone activity in the Wright-Patterson area.

Another individual interviewed reported not being in the area on December 16.

Portions of the investigative narrative are redacted, including identifying information. The released material does not establish that either individual was responsible for the incursions, nor does it establish a connection between the vehicles and the reported aircraft.

Nevertheless, the records reveal that investigators pursued leads involving potential operators on the ground, rather than limiting their efforts to collecting eyewitness accounts of the aircraft themselves.

Conflicting Accounts Within AFOSI’s Own Investigation

The newly released records also contain an unexplained discrepancy within AFOSI’s own investigative summary concerning observations made by local law enforcement during the December 16–17 incursions.

According to the report:

“At 2310 hours, Metro Park Police, Dayton, OH, notified OSI 10 FIS that their patrols observed a sUAS fly from the direction of Colonel Glen Highway, Beavercreek, OH, towards Area B, WPAFB, OH, in the general direction towards the NMUSAF.”

However, further down on the very same page, AFOSI documents an entirely different account:

“OSI 10 FIS coordinated with Metro Parks Police, Dayton, OH, who relayed that none of their patrols spotted any sUAS activity.”

The two statements are contained within the same investigative communication, yet no explanation is provided for the discrepancy.

Was the original sighting subsequently determined to be erroneous? Did the police department retract its initial report? Or did investigators receive conflicting information from different personnel within the department?

The released records do not address these questions, nor do they document any effort to reconcile the two accounts before AFOSI marked the investigative matter closed.

Previously Released FAA Records Raise Additional Questions

The newly released AFOSI investigative records leave unanswered questions when compared with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) documents previously obtained by The Black Vault under FOIA case 2025-04622.

During the same December 16–17 incident investigated by AFOSI and the FBI, the FAA documented between seven and 17 radar targets within 40 miles of the airport. The FAA’s Mandatory Occurrence Report, number 1530847975, categorized the activity as a “Swarm (Multiple UAS aircraft).”

According to the FAA, the Wright-Patterson air traffic control supervisor “reported that security forces on the ground confirmed that the observed targets were drones.”

Despite documenting numerous visual observations, including those made by AFOSI personnel themselves, the newly released investigative communication makes no mention of these radar detections or any analysis of the associated radar data.

Instead, AFOSI documented coordination with Wright-Patterson Airfield Management Operations and Air Traffic Control, stating that both reported they “did not see any aircraft or sUAS in the airspace during the incident.”

The FAA records distinguish between radar detections and visual observations, noting that the targets were detected on radar but were not visually observed from the tower or by aircraft. Whether the radar information was subsequently provided to AFOSI or the FBI, and whether investigators correlated those returns with observations made by military personnel on the ground, remains unanswered.

Also absent from the newly released records are two subsequent sightings documented by the FAA: a silver unmanned aircraft reported near Wright-Patterson on the afternoon of December 17, and a “black cube”-shaped object reported on December 19 approximately 500 feet beneath an aircraft flying at 16,000 feet.

The FAA noted that the aircraft involved in the latter sighting appeared to be conducting a round-trip flight from Wright-Patterson, although the sighting itself occurred well east of the installation.

Neither sighting falls within the periods of drone activity documented in the three newly released AFOSI investigative communications. Their absence does not establish that investigators overlooked the reports, and no released records establish a connection between those subsequent sightings and the earlier incursions.

Whether either event was investigated by the FBI or AFOSI remains unknown.

The FBI’s November 13, 2026, letter identifies the disclosure as its final response to the FOIA request. That determination, however, concerns the material referred by AFOSI and does not establish that the FBI has released all records independently maintained concerning the incidents. The Black Vault has filed another specific case to the FBI to obtain all other records beyond just the AFOSI referred material.

Despite direct observations by AFOSI personnel, joint interviews with the FBI, reported thermal imaging, video evidence and investigative leads involving potential operators, the released records provide no definitive explanation for the incursions.

Nearly two years after the events, the newly disclosed documents provide a more detailed account of what investigators knew and what evidence they collected, but not who was responsible.

item.content:encoded:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has released records documenting the September 21, 2026, air traffic control outage that disrupted operations at major airports across the northeastern United States, including Philadelphia, Newark, and New York-area airports.

The records, obtained by The Black Vault through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), include operational logs from Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), national traffic management records, and facility metrics documenting the effects of the disruption.

However, the November 17, 2026, response also identifies significant limitations in the records provided. Although the request specifically sought technical assessments, maintenance records, documentation of the equipment failures, and information concerning restoration efforts, the FAA stated that the Philadelphia ATCT/TRACON held no responsive records for several of those categories.

The release provides an operational record of the outage and its effects on air traffic management, but does not include a final technical investigation establishing the sequence of equipment failures or the underlying causes.

A Telecommunications Failure Disrupts Northeast Air Traffic

On September 21, 2026, a telecommunications outage affecting Philadelphia TRACON resulted in widespread air traffic restrictions across the Northeast.

 

According to reporting by Reuters, the disruption began after telecommunications infrastructure was damaged in New Jersey, affecting FAA systems supporting air traffic operations. Flights into several major airports were halted for hours while technicians worked to restore service.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford explained during a September 21 news conference that a primary telecommunications circuit had failed. When the FAA attempted to transition to a backup connection, officials discovered that the backup fiber-optic line had also been damaged.

NorthJersey.com quoted Bedford describing the problem:

“Unfortunately, that circuit failed today and when it went to flip into the back-up, we discovered that the back-up fiber had a break, and that fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It’s massive, I’m told.

The reported damaged fiber infrastructure was located between New Brunswick and Newark, New Jersey.

Separately, NJ Transit identified construction activity associated with its Delco Lead project between New Brunswick and North Brunswick. According to a statement reported by CBS Philadelphia, a construction crew accidentally cut into the Verizon fiber-optic line at approximately 9:45 a.m.

NJ Transit stated:

“Preliminary information indicates the crew was operating approximately 10 feet from the utility markings.”

The rail agency also said it was examining the circumstances surrounding the utility markings and the cable damage.

The resulting disruption affected airports including Philadelphia International, Newark Liberty International, John F. Kennedy International, LaGuardia, and Teterboro. Boston Logan also experienced air traffic restrictions.

According to CBS Philadelphia, Philadelphia International Airport had recorded approximately 400 delays and more than 200 cancellations by early that evening.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy subsequently announced that the damaged telecommunications lines had been repaired and that airport operations were resuming, although delays continued as airlines worked through the disruption.

What the Newly Released FAA Records Contain

On September 22, 2026, one day after the outage, The Black Vault submitted a FOIA request seeking five categories of records concerning the incident.

The request sought final incident reports, FAA Technical Operations maintenance and trouble tickets, records establishing the cause of the failures, documentation of operational restrictions, and records concerning the timing of the outages and restoration efforts.

In its November 17 response, the FAA’s Air Traffic Organization, Mission Readiness Services, Eastern Service Center, characterized its determination as a “partial no-records disclosure response.”

The agency explained that the Philadelphia Airport Traffic Control Tower and Terminal Radar Approach Control Quality Control Office had conducted a search of Air Traffic Services records.

For the requested incident reports and equivalent documentation, the FAA stated:

“Facility equipment abnormalities and outages for September 21, 2026, were documented by Air Traffic Services facility personnel on FAA Form 7230-4, Daily Record of Facility Operation for the PHL ATCT/TRACON Area C, which is enclosed.”

The agency added:

“PHL ATCT/TRACON holds no additional records related to this portion of the request.”

The released Daily Record of Facility Operation contains time-stamped entries documenting equipment abnormalities, operational conditions, and actions recorded by facility personnel on September 21.

The release also includes the National Traffic Management Log (NTML), which records traffic management activity, including restrictions and operational adjustments during the disruption.

Additional material consists of an Operations Network (OPSNET) Facility Metrics Report for September 21, providing operational data associated with Philadelphia.

These records offer a way to examine how the outage was managed from the air traffic operations side, separate from the technical investigation into the telecommunications failures themselves.

What Remains Unanswered

The newly released records preserve an official account of the operational disruption experienced by Philadelphia TRACON on September 21, 2026.

They also document the FAA’s traffic management response, including the operational restrictions implemented during the interruption.

The release does not, however, contain a final technical assessment explaining the primary circuit failure, a complete engineering analysis of the backup connection damage, or the requested documentation of equipment restoration and return-to-service testing.

Those subjects were central to the original FOIA request, particularly given the extent of the disruption across multiple airports.

The complete 35-page FOIA package, including the request, FAA response, operational logs, traffic management records, and facility metrics, is preserved below for public examination.

item.content:encoded:
Background

Jeffrey Edward Epstein (January 20, 1953 – August 10, 2019) was an American financier and convicted sex offender. Epstein began his career in finance at the investment bank Bear Stearns before forming his own firm, J. Epstein & Co. Until his conviction for sex crimes in 2008, Epstein was a multimillionaire who was connected with the financial, political, and cultural elite of society.

In April 2005, police of Palm Beach, Florida began investigating Epstein after a parent complained that he molested her 14-year-old daughter. After an investigation, prosecution, and plea negotiations, Epstein pleaded guilty and was convicted by a Florida state court of soliciting a prostitute and of procuring an underage girl for prostitution on June 30, 2008. He served 13 months in custody with work release as part of a plea deal while federal officials had identified 36 girls as young as 14 years old who had been molested.

Epstein was arrested again on July 6, 2019 on federal charges for sex trafficking of minors in Florida and New York. He died on August 10, 2019, reportedly after hanging himself in his Manhattan prison cell. Three weeks earlier, Epstein had been found unconscious in his jail cell with injuries to his neck and placed on suicide watch, which lasted six days and ended twelve days before he died. An autopsy was performed on August 11; the New York City medical examiner’s office announced that it needed more information before the cause of death could be determined, though it is presumed to be suicide.

item.content:encoded:
A September 4, 2026, disruption at San Diego International Airport that delayed hundreds of flights is now documented in newly released Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) records, including air traffic control recordings and two Mandatory Occurrence Reports describing sightings of suspected drones near the airport’s runway.

The records, obtained by The Black Vault through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), provide additional details about what pilots and air traffic controllers reported during the incident, how flight operations were affected, and the involvement of law enforcement. They also reveal a previously unreported detail involving nearby Naval Air Station North Island, where military personnel reportedly were preparing to engage an unauthorized drone. More notably, an air traffic control recording contains a statement indicating that a drone near the military installation may have been shot down.

While the FAA’s written report confirms that North Island personnel communicated their intention to engage an unauthorized drone, the separate reference to a possible shootdown remains unverified. No corroborating military records or public confirmation of such an engagement have been identified, as of the writing of this article. The newly released material raises additional questions about the military’s response to the incident, although the records do not establish whether a drone was actually destroyed, who operated the reported objects, or whether the various sightings involved separate aircraft.

An Afternoon of Disrupted Flights

On Friday, September 4, 2026, San Diego International Airport publicly confirmed that a drone and a weather balloon had been identified in the immediate vicinity of the airport at approximately 2:00 p.m. local time.

The FAA temporarily paused arrivals and departures in response, with the airport reporting that an all-clear was issued at approximately 4:30 p.m.

According to NBC 7 San Diego, airport spokesperson Nicole Hall confirmed the sightings and said that airport operations had resumed following the all-clear. Hall also stated that airport personnel would continue coordinating with the FAA, Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and local law enforcement. TSA law enforcement was investigating the drone activity.

The interruption occurred as Labor Day weekend travel was beginning. NBC 7 reported that approximately 420 flights had been delayed by 6:00 p.m., citing FlightAware, while FAA figures indicated average delays of approximately 122 minutes. Those figures describe the broader disruption and do not establish that every delayed flight was directly attributable to the reported objects.

FAA traffic-management advisories independently document the operational effects. An advisory issued at 21:02 UTC, or 2:02 p.m. Pacific time, warned that aircraft arriving at San Diego could encounter airborne holding of up to 30 minutes because of compacted demand. A subsequent advisory activated diversion-recovery procedures for the airport.

The publicly reported drone and balloon sightings provided the initial explanation for the disruption. The FAA’s subsequently released internal records offer a more detailed account of what personnel were reporting as the incident unfolded.

The FAA Releases Two Incident Reports and Air Traffic Control Recordings

9-4 GC FOIA.wav  (Transcripts: .srt, .txt)

9-4 LC FOIA.wav (Transcripts: .srt, .txt)

The Black Vault submitted its FOIA request on September 10, 2026, seeking records concerning the September 4 incident.

In an October 22, 2026, response under case number 2026-05893, the FAA confirmed that searches had been conducted at San Diego Airport Traffic Control Tower and by the agency’s Quality Control Group.

The FAA identified four responsive records: two audio re-recordings from the tower’s Ground Control and Local Control positions, and two Mandatory Occurrence Reports.

Multiple Pilots Reported an Object Near the Runway

The more extensive occurrence report, SAN-M-2026/09/04-0004, documents activity beginning at 20:54 UTC, corresponding to 1:54 p.m. Pacific time.

Its summary states:

“MULTIPLE TAXIING A/C REPORTED DRONE ABOUT 003 FEET TO 015 FEET DIRECTLY OVER THE RUNWAY DEPARTURE END BETWEEN B7 AND B10. ALL DEPARTURES STOPPED.”

The report uses three-digit altitude notation. The precise altitude associated with this passage is not independently established by the released materials.

The report continues:

“TOWER WAS UNABLE TO GET VISUAL WITH THIS OBJECT BUT AT LEAST 7 PLUS A/C KEPT REPORTING IT.”

At approximately 21:30 UTC, or 2:30 p.m. local time, the tower reported obtaining visual contact with a silver object hovering north of the runway over Taxiway F. The report attributes an additional sighting to a United Airlines flight.

According to the report, a law enforcement helicopter subsequently observed the object:

“ASTREA POLICE HELICOPTER WAS ABLE TO GET A VISUAL WITH THE OBJECT AT 2140Z BUT UNABLE TO GET VIDEO.”

ASTREA is the San Diego County Sheriff’s Department’s aviation unit.

This distinction is important. The FAA report documents a visual observation by the helicopter crew but does not provide imagery from the encounter. The report also does not identify the object’s manufacturer, model, operator, or physical characteristics beyond the reported observations.

The report’s quality-assurance findings state:

“multiple pilots both airborne and taxiing reported a UAS in the vicinity of SAN airport.”

The same findings describe reported altitudes of approximately 300 to 1,500 feet.

The report classified the occurrence as significant and recorded a suspension of operations. It did not identify a verified near-midair collision, aircraft collision, or injury.

A Second Reported Object Near the Departure End

The FAA’s second occurrence report, SAN-M-2026/09/04-0001, focuses on a sighting reported by Southwest Airlines Flight 1562.

The report records the following:

“SWA1562 REPORTED DRONE 1 MILE OFF DEPARTURE END AT 010 FEET NORTH OF RUNWAY. ZEBRA, DEN, HPD NOTIFIED.”

The report’s quality-assurance review provides additional context:

“Pilot reported a UAS in their vicinity at an altitude of approximately 1,000ft. Closest proximity not reported.”

The larger occurrence report also describes this sighting at approximately 22:00 UTC, or 3:00 p.m. Pacific time. It states that the object was silver and that another Southwest Airlines flight reported a similar object eight minutes later.

However, the FAA expressly acknowledged uncertainty about whether these reports involved a different object.

The summary states:

“BUT THIS TIME THE TOWER LOST SIGHT OF OBJECT 1 SO THIS COULD BE POTENTIALLY BE THAT OBJECT.”

The report adds that the ASTREA helicopter returned but was again unable to obtain video.

Consequently, although the FAA documented multiple sightings at different locations, the records do not conclusively establish how many separate objects were involved.

Military Reports From Naval Air Station North Island

One of the additional details in the released records concerns activity at Naval Air Station North Island.

The larger FAA occurrence report contains a separate entry identified as the third object, timed at approximately 21:30 UTC, or 2:30 p.m. Pacific.

It states:

“NAVY NORTH ISLAND CALLED STATING THE MILITARY HAD AN UNATHORUIZED DRONE THEY WERE PREPARING TO ENGAGE.”

The report subsequently identifies DEN, JSEN, ZEBRA, and HPD as having been notified.

This passage documents what the FAA recorded receiving from North Island. It does not establish whether military personnel actually engaged the reported drone, what equipment or methods were contemplated, or whether the object was recovered.

The released materials also do not establish a connection between the reported military activity and the objects observed near San Diego International Airport.

What the Air Traffic Control Transcripts Reveal

The FAA also released recordings from the Local Control and Ground Control positions. The accompanying SRT transcripts reviewed by The Black Vault contain several exchanges that provide further context about the controllers’ response and the uncertainty surrounding the sightings.

The transcripts were not prepared by the FAA, but rather, generated by The Black Vault’s own software designed for this purpose. The agency specifically stated that no responsive transcripts were found. Accordingly, the SRT files should be treated as working transcriptions of the released recordings, rather than independently authenticated verbatim FAA transcripts.

In the Local Control transcript, at approximately 00:06:39 of the recording, a controller announces:

“And for everyone holding for departure, we got a drone, unauthorized drone activity over the runway, so just stand by a couple minutes.”

The Ground Control transcript contains a similar explanation at approximately 00:28:40, when a controller responds to a pilot asking how long the delay might last:

“Not too sure at the moment, this drone is just kind of hanging around in the vicinity and once we get word on its removal or once it’s gone then we can kind of get things going but for the moment we can’t depart just for safety purposes”

These exchanges document controllers communicating a safety-based reason for holding departures while the reported object remained in the vicinity.

Other portions of the transcripts describe efforts to locate and characterize the object.

At approximately 00:11:29 in the Ground Control transcript, one speaker describes its appearance:

“It’s probably metallic color because it’s reflecting a lot of light, almost looks like a silver sphere.”

This description is consistent with the silver appearance recorded in the FAA occurrence reports, but it does not independently establish the object’s identity or whether it was a drone, balloon, or something else.

The transcripts also document uncertainty over reports of an additional object. At approximately 00:46:54 in the Ground Control recording, a speaker states:

“Looks like there might be two drones out there now”

A subsequent exchange questions whether one of the objects could instead have been a helicopter. The transcription includes the response:

“I mean, it’s getting so far away, it could have been a helicopter, we just couldn’t tell”

A Reference to a Drone Being Shot Down

The Ground Control transcript also contains an exchange concerning Naval Air Station North Island that warrants attention, although its contents remain unverified.

At approximately 00:55:52, a speaker is transcribed as saying:

“I think there’s one over North Island that just got shot down.”

“I don’t know what they can do, but one over North Island got shot down.”

This exchange is distinct from the written FAA occurrence report, which states only that military personnel were preparing to engage an unauthorized drone.

The released documents do not confirm that a drone was shot down. The statement in the transcript should therefore be understood as an unverified assertion made during the incident, not a confirmed military action.

The recordings provide no independently established outcome for the reported North Island activity.

What Remains Unanswered

The FAA records substantiate that numerous pilots reported suspected unmanned aircraft activity near San Diego International Airport, that controllers suspended departures, and that law enforcement personnel were involved in attempts to observe the objects.

The released records leave several questions unresolved, including the identities and operators of the reported objects, the number of separate drones involved, whether the weather balloon identified in the airport’s public statement corresponds to any of the sightings documented in the FAA reports, and the outcome of the military’s reported response at North Island.

The documents and associated air traffic control recordings are preserved in The Black Vault’s document archive, and are available below.

Background

Movements for civil rights were a worldwide series of political movements for equality before the law that peaked in the 1960s. In many situations it took the form of campaigns of civil resistance aimed at achieving change through nonviolent forms of resistance. In some situations it was accompanied, or followed, by civil unrest and armed rebellion. The process was long and tenuous in many countries, and many of these movements did not fully achieve their goals, although the efforts of these movements did lead to improvements in the legal rights of previously oppressed groups of people.

Below are files of prominent people and events.

 

Declassified Civil Rights Movement FBI Files

The following file is archived here for historical reference, and may contain language and references that are offensive to some people.

The Communist Party and the Negro, February 1953 – [ 114 Pages, 4.75 MB ] – Excerpt: Since its organization in this country in 1919, the Communist Party, USA, has devoted an inordinate portion of its time, funds, propaganda and personnel to recruiting members from among the fifteen million Negroes who comprise almost ten percent of our total population. The failure of its efforts in this respect is best attested to by the fact that it can be estimated that there are at present only 1,994 active, disciplined, dues-paying Negro members in the Communist Party. Of course, in addition to this figure,  there are approximately 18,000 other Negroes who have some contact with the Party, and its front groups, and who, to a certain degree, influenced directly or -indirectly by its program, propaganda and agitation.

 

16th Street Baptist Church Bombing – [ 242 Pages, 12.45 MB ] – The 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama was bombed on Sunday, September 15, 1963 as an act of racially motivated terrorism. The explosion at the African-American church, which killed four girls, marked a turning point in the United States 1960s Civil Rights Movement and contributed to support for passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Abdullah, Hakim Abdullah – NARA Release – [27 Pages, 1.3MB]
Abdullah, Hakim Abdullah – FBI Release – [10 Pages, 3.2MB] – Hakim Abdullah Jamal (March 28, 1931 – May 1, 1973) was the name adopted by American activist Allen Donaldson, who was a cousin of Malcolm X and later became an associate of Michael X. Jamal wrote From the Dead Level, a memoir of his life and memories of Malcolm X. Jamal was romantically involved with several high-profile women, notably Jean Seberg, Diana Athill, and Gale Benson.
Abernathy, Ralph – [1,558 Pages, 52MB] – Ralph David Abernathy, Sr. (March 11, 1926 – April 17, 1990) was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, a minister, and Martin Luther King Jr.’s closest friend. In 1955, he collaborated with King to create the Montgomery Improvement Association, which would lead to the Montgomery Bus Boycott. In 1957, Abernathy co-founded, and was an executive board member of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). Following the assassination of King, Abernathy became president of the SCLC. As president of the SCLC, he led the Poor People’s Campaign in Washington, D.C. during 1968. Abernathy also served as an advisory committee member of the Congress on Racial Equality (CORE). He later returned to the ministry, and in 1989 — the year before his death — Abernathy wrote, And the Walls Came Tumbling Down: An Autobiography, a controversial autobiography about his and King’s involvement in the civil rights movement.
Allen, Lillie Belle – [ 45 Pages, 1.39 MB ] – On July 21, Lillie Belle Allen, a black woman from Aiken, S.C., who was visiting York with her parents, was riding in a car driven by her sister, Hattie Dickinson. Dickinson turned the car onto North Newberry Street and was looking for a grocery store when she saw a man with a gun leaning out of a second-story window. Multiple members of two all-white gangs, the Newberry Street Boys and the Girarders, were on the street that night, and many of them were armed. Dickinson began to turn around in the intersection of Newberry Street and Gay Avenue but the car stalled. As more armed white men began coming onto their porches, Dickinson panicked. Her parents, who were in the back seat, beging praying. Her older sister, Lillie Belle Allen, jumped out of the car to get to the driver’s seat and take the wheel. She flailed her arms screaming, “Don’t shoot!” Multiple shooters opened fire from the street, rooftops and windows, fatally wounding Allen. More than one hundred rounds were fired at the car, and Allen was shot by several different types of bullets.
Allen,  Louie – [ 93 Pages, 7.87 MB ] – Louis Allen (April 25, 1919 – January 31, 1964) was an African American logger and civil rights activist in the small town of Liberty, Mississippi. He allegedly witnessed the murder of a fellow activist by a white state legislator, and was himself murdered when he approached federal authorities about the killing. Despite a consensus among investigators that Allen was killed by Amite County’s sheriff, no one has been prosecuted for the murder.

 

Anderson, Marian – [ 122 Pages,  8.93MB ] – Marian Anderson (February 27, 1897 – April 8, 1993) was an African-American contralto and one of the most celebrated singers of the twentieth century. Music critic Alan Blyth said “Her voice was a rich, vibrant contralto of intrinsic beauty.” Most of her singing career was spent performing in concert and recital in major music venues and with famous orchestras throughout the United States and Europe between 1925 and 1965. Although offered roles with many important European opera companies, Anderson declined, as she had no training in acting. She preferred to perform in concert and recital only. She did, however, perform opera arias within her concerts and recitals. She made many recordings that reflected her broad performance repertoire of everything from concert literature to lieder to opera to traditional American songs and spirituals. Anderson became an important figure in the struggle for black artists to overcome racial prejudice in the United States during the mid-twentieth century.
Barrett, Richard – [ 242 Pages, 12.45 MB ] –  Richard Anthony Barrett (1934-2010) was a leader of several white supremacist groups. In 1987, following a rally in Cummings, Georgia, Barrett received a death threat that he reported to the FBI.
This release consists of five different investigations conducted between 1967 and 2003 in which Barrett was either a subject of the case or was mentioned in another investigation
Black Guerilla Family – [ 456 Pages, 17.18 MB ] – The Black Guerrilla Family (also known as the Black Family or the Black Vanguard) is a prison and street gang founded in 1966 by George Jackson and W.L.
Nolen while they were incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison in Marin County, California, north of San Francisco.
 Chavez, Cesar – [ File #1 | File #2 | File #3 | File #4 | File #5 | File #6 | File #7 | File #8 | File #9 | File #10 | File #11 | File #12 | File #13 | File #14 | File #15 | File #16 | File #17 ] – Cesar Chavez (born César Estrada Chávez, (March 31, 1927 – April 23, 1993) was an American farm worker, labor leader and civil rights activist, who, with Dolores Huerta, co-founded the National Farm Workers Association (later the United Farm Workers union, UFW).

 Dee, Ruby [1 Pages, 0.5MB] – Ruby Dee (October 27, 1922 – June 11, 2014) was an American actress, poet, playwright, screenwriter, journalist and civil rights activist. She is perhaps best known for originating the role of “Ruth Younger” in the stage and film versions of A Raisin in the Sun (1961). Her other notable film roles include The Jackie Robinson Story (1950), and Do the Right Thing (1989).

Unfortunately, the National Archives found hundreds of pages on Ruby Dee, but are charging me .80 cents per page. I am archiving this here so others know this file is available either at the NARA branch itself (reference this FOIA request and file number) or via payment. If you’d like to “sponsor” the retrieval of this document, please CONTACT me.
 DuBois, William E.B. – [ File #1 | File #2 | File #3 | File #4 | File #5 ] – William E.B. DuBois, former Director of Publications of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, was of interest to the FBI due to his affiliation with communist front groups.
Evers, Medgar – [ 236 Pages, 17.55 MB ] – Medgar Wiley Evers (July 2, 1925 – June 12, 1963) was an African-American civil rights activist from Mississippi involved in efforts to overturn segregation at the University of Mississippi. After returning from overseas military service in World War II and completing his secondary education, he became active in the civil rights movement. He became a field secretary for the NAACP.
Fard, Wallace – The FBI’s “Vault” Release – [ File # 1 | File # 2 | File # 3 | File # 4 | File # 5 | File # 6 | File # 7 ]
Fard, Wallace – FBI Release #1 (Not on The Vault) [995 Pages, 75MB] – Miscellaneous information about Wallace D. Fard, who is said to be the original founder of the Black Muslim movement.
Farmer, James L. – [ 338 Pages, 18.58 MB ] – James Leonard Farmer, Jr. (January 12, 1920 – July 9, 1999) was a civil rights activist and leader in the American Civil Rights Movement. He was the initiator and organizer of the 1961 Freedom Ride, which eventually led to the desegregation of inter-state transportation in the United States. In 1942, Farmer co-founded the Committee of Racial Equality, which later became the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), an organization that sought to bring an end to racial segregation in the United States through nonviolence. Farmer was the organization’s first leader, serving as the national chairman from 1942 to 1944. He was an honorary vice chairman in the Democratic Socialists of America.
 Freedom Riders – [ File #1 | File #2 | File #3 | File #4 | File #5 | File #6 | File #7 | File #8 | File #9 | File #10 | File #11 | File #12 | File #13 | File #14 | File #15 | File #16 | File #17 | File #18 | File #19 | File #20 | File #21 | File #22 ] [ 4,285 Total Pages] – Freedom Riders were civil rights activists who rode interstate buses into the segregated southern United States in 1961 and following years to challenge the non-enforcement of the United States Supreme Court decisions Irene Morgan v. Commonwealth of Virginia (1946) and Boynton v. Virginia (1960), which ruled that segregated public buses were unconstitutional. The Southern states had ignored the rulings and the federal government did nothing to enforce them. The first Freedom Ride left Washington, D.C., on May 4, 1961, and was scheduled to arrive in New Orleans on May 17.
Geiger, H. Jack – [24 Pages, 1.2MB] – Herman J. Geiger (November 11, 1925 – December 28, 2020), known as H. Jack Geiger, was an American physician and civil rights activist. He was a leader in the field of social medicine, the philosophy that doctors had a responsibility to treat the social as well as medical conditions that adversely affected patients’ health, famously (and controversially) writing prescriptions for food for impoverished patients suffering from malnutrition. Geiger came to embody the idea of the responsibility of a physician to do something about what is now known as the social determinants of health, believing that medicine could be an instrument of social change. He served patients’ medical needs as well as social and economic necessities, which he believed were in large part responsible for the health problems communities faced. He was one of the doctors to bring the community health center model to the United States, starting a network that serves 28 million low-income patients as of 2020.
Gregory, Richard “Dick” Claxton – [3,384 Pages, 339.4MB] – Richard Claxton Gregory (October 12, 1932 – August 19, 2017) was an African-American comedian, civil rights activist, social critic, writer, entrepreneur, conspiracy theorist, and occasional actor. During the turbulent 1960s, Gregory became a pioneer in stand-up comedy for his “no-holds-barred” sets, in which he mocked bigotry and racism. He performed primarily to black audiences at segregated clubs until 1961, when he became the first black comedian to successfully cross over to white audiences, appearing on television and putting out comedy record albums.  Gregory was at the forefront of political activism in the 1960s, when he protested the Vietnam War and racial injustice. He was arrested multiple times and went on many hunger strikes. He later became a speaker and author, primarily promoting spirituality.  Gregory died of heart failure at a Washington, D.C., hospital at age 84 in August 2017.
Hamer, Fannie Lou – FBI Release #1 – [554 Pages, 28.68 MB]
Hamer, Fannie Lou – FBI Release #2 – [167 Pages, 15MB] – Fannie Lou Hamer (1917-1977) was a voting rights activist and civil rights leader. In June 1963, she and several other voting rights activists were arrested at a Mississippi bus station. This release concerns the FBI’s investigation into possible civil rights violations relating to that arrest.
Hampton, Fred – [194 Pages, 8.01 MB] – Fred Hampton (August 30, 1948 – December 4, 1969) was an African-American activist and deputy chairman of the Illinois chapter of the Black Panther Party (BPP). He was killed while sleeping in his apartment during a raid by a tactical unit of the Cook County, Illinois State’s Attorney’s Office (SAO), in conjunction with the Chicago Police Department (CPD) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Hampton’s murder was chronicled in the 1971 documentary film The Murder of Fred Hampton, as well as an episode of the critically acclaimed documentary series Eyes on the Prize.
Hayden, Tom – FBI Vault Release – [608 Pages, 31MB]
Hayden, Tom – FBI Release #1 – [181 Pages, 13MB]
Hayden, Tom – FBI Release #2 – [273 Pages, 51.2MB] – Thomas Emmet Hayden (December 11, 1939 – October 23, 2016) was an American social and political activist, author, and politician. Hayden was best known for his role as an anti-war, civil rights, and intellectual activist in the 1960s, authoring the Port Huron Statement and standing trial in the Chicago Seven case. In later years, he ran for political office numerous times, winning seats in both the California Assembly and California Senate. At the end of his life he was the director of the Peace and Justice Resource Center in Los Angeles County. He was married to Jane Fonda for 17 years, and is the father of actor Troy Garity.
Hedgeman, Anna – [251 Pages, 52.4MB]
Hedgeman, Anna – [11 Pages, 2MB] – Anna Arnold Hedgeman (1899-1990) was an influential African American civil rights advocate, educator, and public servant. She was a pioneering force in the fight for racial and gender equality, dedicating her life to social justice and community service. Hedgeman was the first African American woman to hold a mayoral cabinet position in New York City under Mayor Robert F. Wagner Jr., where she worked on issues of employment, housing, and education. She played a significant role in organizing the 1963 March on Washington, contributing to the historic event that brought attention to the Civil Rights Movement. Her work with organizations such as the National Urban League and the National Council of Churches, along with her efforts in education and politics, left an indelible mark on American society.
 Hudson, Winson– [189 Pages, 7.6MB] – Winson Hudson (1916–2004) was a dedicated civil rights activist from Mississippi whose lifelong commitment to justice helped transform voting rights in the American South. Born in Leake County, she became deeply involved in the movement through her work with the NAACP, where she served as president of the local chapter for more than 35 years. Hudson played a key role in registering Black voters despite facing threats, economic retaliation, and violence. She was also instrumental in desegregating schools in her community, courageously filing lawsuits that challenged entrenched racial barriers. Her memoir, Mississippi Harmony: Memoirs of a Freedom Fighter, co-written with Constance Curry, documents her tireless fight for equality and the personal sacrifices she endured to ensure future generations could live in a more just America.
Hooks, Benjamin – [223 Pages, 10.65 MB] – Benjamin Lawson Hooks (1925-2010) was a civil rights leader who served as the director of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) for more than a decade. This release consists of a background investigation file with materials dated 1972-1980 and several investigative files concerning threats against Hooks or the NAACP between 1987 and 1990.
Jones, Claudia – [805 Pages, 42.85 MB] – Claudia Cumberbatch Jones (15 February 1915—24 December 1964) was a Trinidadian journalist, who became a political activist and black nationalist through Communism.
Kasper, John – FBI Release #1 –  [2,787 Pages, 206MB]
Kasper, John – FBI Vault Releases #1-6 –  [2,780 Pages, 135MB] – John Kasper was an American far-right activist and bookseller known for his vehement opposition to the racial integration of schools following the Supreme Court’s landmark decision in Brown v. Board of Education. Born in 1929, Kasper gained national notoriety in the mid-1950s for his involvement in anti-integration protests, most notably in Clinton, Tennessee, where his incendiary speeches contributed to escalating racial tensions and violence. Despite several arrests and convictions for incitement to riot, Kasper remained a vocal proponent of segregation, often associating himself with the doctrine of “massive resistance” against federal desegregation mandates. A controversial figure throughout his life, Kasper also embraced and propagated the works of American poet Ezra Pound, whose economic and political views echoed his own nativist ideologies.
King, Coretta Scott – [ 976 Pages, 19.76MB ] – Coretta Scott King (April 27, 1927 – January 30, 2006) was an American author, activist, and civil rights leader. The widow of Martin Luther King, Jr., Coretta Scott King helped lead the African-American Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s. Mrs. King played a prominent role in the years after her husband’s 1968 assassination when she took on the leadership of the struggle for racial equality herself and became active in the Women’s Movement and the LGBT rights movement.
 King, Rodney – [ 725 Pages, 53 MB ] – Rodney Glen King (1965-2012) was the victim of an abusive arrest by Los Angeles police officers on March 3, 1991. Two officers involved in the arrest were found guilty of depriving King of his civil rights. This 725-page release of material from the FBI’s color of law investigation consists almost exclusively of news clippings related to the case.
 King, Jr., Martin Luther [226 Pages, 4MB] – Martin Luther King Jr. (born Michael King Jr., January 15, 1929 – April 4, 1968) was an American Baptist minister and activist who was a leader in the Civil Rights Movement. He is best known for his role in the advancement of civil rights using nonviolent civil disobedience based on his Christian beliefs.
Ku Klux Klan – [676 Pages, 22.57MB]
Ku Klux Klan – (Russ Kick Collection) – [133 Pages, 22.4MB] – The first Ku Klux Klan flourished in the Southern United States in the late 1860s, then died out by the early 1870s. Members adopted white costumes: robes, masks, and conical hats, designed to be outlandish and terrifying, and to hide their identities. The second KKK flourished nationwide in the early and mid-1920s, and adopted the same costumes and code words as the first Klan, while introducing cross burnings. The third KKK emerged after World War II and was associated with opposing the Civil Rights Movement and progress among minorities. The second and third incarnations of the Ku Klux Klan made frequent reference to the USA’s “Anglo-Saxon” blood, harking back to 19th-century nativism and claiming descent from the original 18th-century British colonial revolutionaries.
Lee, George Washington – [20 Pages, 13.7MB] – George Washington Lee (December 25, 1903 – May 7, 1955) was an African-American civil rights leader, minister, and entrepreneur. He was a vice president of the Regional Council of Negro Leadership and head of the Belzoni, Mississippi, branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. He was assassinated in 1955 for organizing African Americans to try to register to vote. Since 1890 they had been effectively disenfranchised in Mississippi due to a new state constitution; other states across the South passed similar acts and constitutions, excluding millions of people from the political system and establishing one-party states.
 Lingo, Albert J. – [90 Pages, 29.88 MB] – Colonel Albert J. Lingo, also known as Al Lingo (January 22, 1910 – August 19, 1969) was a career Alabama Highway Patrolman who served as Director of the Alabama Department of Public Safety from 1963 to 1965, including the turbulent early 1960s years marked by marches and demonstrations that characterized the civil rights movement in the U.S. South. Lingo’s service under Alabama governor George Wallace with regard to the Selma to Montgomery marches has been characterized in a negative light, though Lingo himself disputed that characterization, stating that he was following orders as required by his oath of office.
He resigned as director effective October 1, 1965, and later ran for election to be sheriff of Jefferson County, Alabama; he died at age 59 on August 17, 1969.
(Source: Ernie Lazar)
Liuzzo, Viola – [ 1,535 Pages, 76.47 MB ] – Viola Fauver Gregg Liuzzo (April 11, 1925 – March 25, 1965) was a Unitarian Universalist civil rights activist from Michigan, who was murdered by Ku Klux Klan members after the 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches in Alabama.
One of the Klansmen in the car from which the shots were fired was a Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) informant. Liuzzo’s name is one of those inscribed on a civil rights memorial in the state capital. She died at the age of 39.
Lowery, Joseph Echols – Cross References – [80 Pages, 41MB] – Joseph Echols Lowery (October 6, 1921 – March 27, 2020) was an American minister in the United Methodist Church and leader in the civil rights movement. He founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference with Martin Luther King Jr. and others, serving as its vice president, later chairman of the board, and from 1977 to 1997 its president. Lowery participated in most of the major activities of the civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s, and continued his civil rights work into the 21st century.
He was called the “Dean of the Civil Rights Movement.”
  Malcolm X – [ Part 01 | Part 02 | Part 03 ] – Malcom X was the Minister of the Nation of Islam up to March 1964.
He left the Nation of Islam and formed the Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity. Malcom X was assassinated in 1965 while delivering a speech in New York City. Norman Butler, Thomas Johnson and Talmage Hayer were convicted of Malcom X’s murder and all three were sentenced to life in prison. The FBI investigated Malcom X to verify communist influence.
Mississippi Burning (MIBURN) – [1,049 Pages, 55.13 MB] – Three American civil rights’ workers, James Earl Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael “Mickey” Schwerner, were shot at close range on the night of June 21–22, 1964 by members of the Mississippi White Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, the Neshoba County’s Sheriff Office and the Philadelphia Police Department located in Philadelphia, Mississippi. The three had been working on the “Freedom Summer” campaign, attempting to register African Americans to vote. Their murders sparked national outrage and a massive federal investigation. The Federal Bureau of Investigation referred to this investigation as Mississippi Burning (MIBURN), and eventually found the bodies 44 days later in an earthen dam near the murder site. After the state government refused to prosecute, the federal government initially charged 18 individuals but was only able to secure convictions for seven of them, who received relatively minor sentences for their actions. However, outrage over their deaths assisted in the passing of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Moore’s Ford Lynching – [3,787 Pages, 235MB] – The Moore’s Ford Lynchings, also known as the 1946 Georgia lynching, refers to the July 25, 1946, murders of four young African Americans by a mob of White men. Tradition says that the murders were committed on Moore’s Ford Bridge in Walton and Oconee counties between Monroe and Watkinsville, but the four victims, two married couples, were shot and killed on a nearby dirt road. The case attracted national attention and catalyzed large protests in Washington, DC and New York City. President Harry Truman created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights and his administration introduced anti-lynching legislation in Congress, but could not get it past the Southern Democratic bloc. The FBI investigated for four months in 1946, the first time it had been ordered to investigate a civil rights case, but it was unable to discover sufficient evidence to bring any charges. In the 1990s publicity about the cold case led to a new investigation. The state of Georgia and the FBI finally closed their cases in December 2017, again unable to prosecute any suspect. The lynching victims — George W. and Mae Murray Dorsey, and Roger and Dorothy Malcom — have been commemorated by a community memorial service in 1998, a state historical marker placed in 1999 at the site of the attack (Georgia’s first official recognition of a lynching), and an annual re-enactment held since 2005. According to the 2015 report by the Equal Justice Initiative on lynchings in the Southern United States, Georgia has the second-highest number of documented lynchings.
NAACP (Summary) – [732 Pages, 26.06 MB] – The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) is an African-American civil rights organization in the United States, formed in 1909. Its mission is “to ensure the political, educational, social, and economic equality of rights of all persons and to eliminate racial hatred and racial discrimination”. Its name, retained in accordance with tradition, uses the once common term colored people. The NAACP bestows the annual Image Awards for achievement in the arts and entertainment, and the annual Spingarn Medals for outstanding positive achievement of any kind, on deserving black Americans. It has its headquarters in Baltimore, Maryland.
Nation of Islam – [ 321 Pages, 14.26 MB ] – The Nation of Islam (NOI) is a syncretic new religious movement founded in Detroit, Michigan by Wallace D. Fard Muhammad in July 1930. The Nation of Islam’s stated goals are to improve the spiritual, mental, social, and economic condition of African Americans in the United States and all of humanity. Its critics accuse it of being black supremacist[2] and antisemitic. The Southern Poverty Law Center states NOI’s “theology of innate black superiority over whites and the deeply racist, anti-Semitic and anti-gay rhetoric of its leaders have earned the NOI a prominent position in the ranks of organized hate.”
  National Council of Churches – [ File #1 51.71MB | File #1A 37.24MB | File #2 17.90MB | File #3 16.69MB | File #4 16.87MB | File #5 28.59MB | File #6 26.53MB | File #7 18.98MB | File #8 32.84MB | File #9 24.15MB | File #10 30.77MB | File #11 23.28MB | File #12 30.71MB | File #13 15.52MB | File #14 26.67MB | File #15 23.94MB | File #16 30.00MB | File #17 16.40MB | File #18 25.32MB | File #19 26.51MB | File #20 21.98MB | File #21 31.37MB | File #22 26.55MB | File #23 17.92MB | File #24 20.96MB | File #25 18.95MB | File #26 16.76MB | File #27 20.66MB | File #28 15.41MB | File #29 20.38MB  | File #30 16.50MB ] – [ 6,530 Total Pages ] – The National Council of the Churches of Christ in the USA, usually identified as the National Council of Churches (NCC), is an ecumenical partnership of 37 Christian faith groups in the United States. Its member denominations, churches, conventions, and archdioceses include Mainline Protestant, Orthodox, African American, Evangelical, and historic peace churches. Together, they encompass more than 100,000 local congregations and 45 million adherents. It began as the Federal Council of Churches in 1908, and expanded through merger with several other ecumenical organizations to become the National Council of Churches in 1950. The NCC’s influence peaked in the 1950s, deriving its strength from a commitment to ecumenism, while the NCC’s strident antiwar position against the Vietnam War in the 1960s alienated the laity leading to a decline in influence thereafter. (Source: Ernie Lazar)
 Parker, Mack Charles – [ 377 Pages, 20.58 MB ] – Mack Charles Parker (1936 – April 24, 1959) was an African-American victim of lynching in the United States. He was accused of ramping a pregnant white woman in northern Pearl River County, Mississippi. Three days before he was to stand trial, he was kidnapped from his jail cell in the Pearl River County Courthouse by a mob, beaten and shot. His body was found in the Pearl River, 20 miles west of Poplarville, 10 days later. Despite evidence compiled by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and indictment by a federal grand jury, the men who killed him were released.
 Perez, Leander – [ 285 Pages, 19.49 MB ] – Leander Henry Perez, Sr. (July 16, 1891 – March 19, 1969), was the Democratic political boss of Plaquemines and St. Bernard parishes in southeastern Louisiana during the middle third of the 20th century. Officially, he served as a district judge, later as district attorney, and as president of the Plaquemines Parish Commission Council. He was known for his staunch support of segregation.
  Randolph, A. Phillip – [ File #1 7.06MB | File #2 17.38MB ] [ 265 Total Pages ] – Asa Philip Randolph (April 15, 1889 – May 16, 1979) was a leader in the African-American civil-rights movement, the American labor movement and socialist political parties. He organized and led the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, the first predominantly black labor union. In the early civil-rights movement, Randolph led the March on Washington Movement, which convinced President Franklin D. Roosevelt to issue Executive Order 8802 in 1941, banning discrimination in the defense industries during World War II. After the war Randolph pressured President Harry S. Truman to issue Executive Order 9981 in 1948, ending segregation in the armed services. (Source: Ernie Lazar)

Once this was done, the next step involved recourse to theoretical physics in order to explain the character of the time-space dimension and the means by which expanded human consciousness transcends it in achieving Gateway’s objectives. Finally~ I again found it necessary to Use physics to bring the whole phenomenon of out-of-body states into the language of physical science to remove the stigma of its occult connotations, and put it in a frame of reference suited to objective assessment.”

item.content:encoded:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) released 20 pages of training materials concerning the collection, processing, and analysis of biological evidence following fatal aviation accidents. The records were released on October 12, 2023, in response to Freedom of Information Act request, which sought presentation slides and a syllabus for the training course Mass Fatalities for Medicolegal Professionals (TDA403). In its response, the FAA stated: “Presentation slides were discovered during the search for records pertaining to this request. No syllabus was found, all training in this course was derived from these slides as presented.”

The released materials include presentations concerning the FAA’s Bioaeronautical Sciences Research Laboratory (BSRL) and its Autopsy Program Team, both associated with the Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (CAMI) in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. These programs support investigations of fatal aviation accidents by coordinating autopsy documentation and conducting forensic toxicological examinations. According to the FAA, its aviation safety responsibilities include collecting medical and pathological information to help identify factors contributing to aircraft accidents. A 2020 FAA technical report, Comparative Evaluation of Forensic Toxicology Findings, 2012–2016, further documents how CAMI’s forensic laboratories and Autopsy Program Team support both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

The first portion of the release, containing presentation slides dated October 1, 2014, describes the laboratory’s handling of biological specimens collected following fatal aircraft accidents. It covers specialized collection kits known as “TOX-BOXes,” chain-of-custody documentation, specimen identification, laboratory storage, and testing for substances including alcohol, carbon monoxide, and various prescription and controlled drugs. The presentation also describes quality assurance procedures, including blind analytical testing, laboratory accreditation, and independent review. These materials provide a historical record of the laboratory’s documented procedures at the time of the presentation.

The second portion addresses the FAA’s Autopsy Program Team and its coordination with medical examiners, coroners, accident investigators, and the NTSB. It describes how the FAA obtains autopsy reports, identifies deceased pilots, and reviews medical evidence that may be relevant to an accident investigation. One instructional case example concerns a fatal light-sport aircraft accident in which an initial decision not to conduct an autopsy was reconsidered. According to the presentation, the subsequent examination identified severe coronary artery disease, including a complete blockage of the left anterior descending coronary artery, and classified the manner of death as natural. The example illustrates the importance of medical findings in examining circumstances surrounding aviation fatalities.

item.content:encoded:
Larry W. Bryant was a UFO researcher, writer, and government transparency advocate who pursued federal records through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). His work included efforts to obtain documents concerning unidentified flying objects, intelligence activities, and government accountability. Bryant also contributed to UFO Magazine, where he examined government records and controversies involving UFO research. His correspondence with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) provides a historical record of his efforts to obtain information and challenge agency disclosure decisions.

This collection, released by the CIA under FOIA case F-2021-02420, contains historical correspondence, administrative records, appeals, and other materials associated with Bryant’s dealings with the agency. Among the subjects addressed are UFO investigations, alleged intelligence operations, and disputes over the CIA’s handling of information requests. The documents include correspondence concerning the agency’s searches, withholding decisions, fee assessments, and Bryant’s attempts to obtain recognition as a representative of the news media.

One notable portion concerns Bryant’s efforts to obtain records associated with the November 1986 Japan Airlines UFO encounter over Alaska and a subsequent meeting reportedly held at Federal Aviation Administration headquarters in 1987. In a September 30, 2008, response, the CIA stated that there was “no organized CIA effort to do research in connection with UFO phenomena” and that the agency had not maintained an organized UFO intelligence collection effort since the 1950s. Subsequent correspondence documents the reopening of Bryant’s request in 2009 and the CIA’s decision to recognize his news media fee status for that particular case. The collection also includes records concerning litigation arising from the dispute.

Other correspondence concerns Bryant’s attempts to obtain CIA records about John Joseph McCarthy Jr., his alleged intelligence activities, and Project CHERRY. In September 2004, the CIA invoked FOIA exemptions concerning classified information and intelligence sources and methods, refusing to confirm or deny the existence of records that would reveal a covert relationship. Subsequent processing resulted in a determination that no responsive records were located, which the CIA upheld on appeal in 2006. Additional materials concern Bryant’s interest in UFO skeptic Philip J. Klass, including a published discussion of FBI records obtained through FOIA.
