item.content:encoded:
Records released by the National Security Agency to The Black Vault in September 2025, and now being published online by The Black Vault, provide additional details about a 1992 Pentagon effort to examine Cold War reconnaissance losses and determine whether missing American personnel may have fallen into the hands of the Soviet Union, China or North Korea.

The records include historical summaries of U.S. reconnaissance incidents and aircraft losses, along with a June 1992 memorandum concerning a Joint Staff effort to examine Cold War POW/MIA cases. Much of the history of the underlying reconnaissance incidents has been documented previously. The significance of the material is instead found in the internal Pentagon discussion surrounding those losses and the questions officials were examining decades later.

Among the most notable passages is a statement that, for some losses, the government’s “official” explanation and what actually happened could represent “two different stories.”

The documents do not establish that missing U.S. servicemen survived in foreign custody. Nor do they establish that official explanations for particular aircraft losses were false. They document questions Pentagon officials were examining in 1992, and some portions of which remain classified today.

A 1992 Joint Staff Review of Cold War POW/MIA Cases

One of the most notable records is a memorandum dated June 17, 1992, titled “JOINT STAFF EFFORT ON COLD WAR POW/MIA ISSUE.”

The memorandum describes a meeting chaired by Maj. Gen. Ryan concerning a task from the Secretary of Defense. According to the document, the effort involved:

“a listing of missing U.S. personnel who may have been captured by the former Soviet Union, PRC or North Korea.”

The memorandum states that downed U.S. reconnaissance assets represented the “most likely candidates,” although possible seaborne losses were also under consideration. CIA and NSA representatives were asked to participate and contribute information.

According to the memorandum, Ryan advised participants that information developed through the effort eventually “will be made public” in some form. Intelligence-community information could be discussed separately.

The document records his position:

“we owe the SecDef as honest a picture as we can present.”

The memorandum also records a separate request from Adm. Cramer:

“Separately, ADM Cramer has asked if we have ‘anything to add to the list or any SIGINT confirming that Soviets have U.S. prisoners.'”

“The ‘Official’ U.S. Explanation”

The memorandum becomes particularly notable in its description of what information officials wanted examined.

It states:

“the ‘official’ U.S. explanation for some of our losses and what really happened might be two different stories.”

The next sentence reads:

“Gen Ryan stressed that this group needs to know the truth.”

The document does not identify in that passage which specific losses prompted the observation. It also does not explain how an official account might have differed from what actually occurred.

Material immediately following this discussion remains withheld in the version released to The Black Vault.

21 Aircraft Loss Incidents and 131 Unaccounted-For Servicemen

Another record, titled “COLD WAR AIRCRAFT LOSSES,” summarizes information supplied by the Air Force and Navy concerning 21 loss incidents between April 1950 and April 1969.

The document separates those incidents into several categories. Four involved cases in which all crew members were recovered and the matter was considered resolved. Six had been presented to the Russians and required additional information. Three involved losses off the coast of the People’s Republic of China. Five had few details available concerning the loss. Two involved partial recovery of crews, and one involved a loss off the Korean coast.

The document then states:

“For the known losses: 131 unaccounted for servicemen.”

The accompanying table identifies Cold War aircraft losses involving a number of platforms, including the Privateer, B-29, P2V, RB-50, C-130, U-2 and RB-47.

A Broader History of U.S. Reconnaissance Incidents

The records also contain the Airborne Reconnaissance Incident History that was at the center of The Black Vault’s original FOIA request.

A Joint Staff Action Processing Form dated June 5, 1992, describes the purpose of the paper as providing a summary of approximately 30 airborne reconnaissance missions during the 1949-1960 period that resulted in international incidents and/or the loss of manned aircraft.

According to the document:

“During the period 1949-1960, there were 32 airborne reconnaissance missions flown which resulted in international incidents and the loss of 13 manned aircraft platforms.”

The pages that follow provide a chronology of encounters involving U.S. reconnaissance aircraft and Soviet, Chinese and North Korean forces.

The release also includes a continuation covering 1961 through 1973.

That section states that after centralized management of reconnaissance activities began in 1960, there was a “significant decrease in reconnaissance-related incidents.” It identifies three losses during the later period: the U-2 shot down over Cuba during the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, the capture of USS Pueblo off North Korea in 1968, and the EC-121 shot down over the Sea of Japan in 1969.

The accompanying chronology documents additional encounters involving U.S. reconnaissance platforms and foreign military forces during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Some of the Record Is Still Classified

Despite the age of both the Cold War incidents and the 1992 review, the FOIA production released to The Black Vault is not complete.

In its September 29, 2025, response, NSA stated that it had “no objection to the release of the NSA equities.” Other information, however, was referred to the Office of the Secretary of Defense-Joint Staff, or OSD-JS (now the Office of the Secretary of War-Joint Staff).

According to NSA, OSD-JS determined that the information remains properly classified under Executive Order 13526 and continues to warrant classification at the SECRET level.

The response states that disclosure:

“could reasonably be expected to cause grave damage to the national security.”

NSA therefore withheld the information under FOIA Exemption (b)(1). Other material was withheld under Exemption (b)(6) to protect personal privacy.

One of the OSD-JS deletions occurs directly after the 1992 memorandum’s discussion of the possibility that an “official” explanation for some losses and “what really happened” could be different.

The historical summary covering 1961 through 1973 also contains information withheld by OSD-JS.

The records were released to The Black Vault in September 2025 after a FOIA request specifically sought material excluded from an earlier NSA release as “non responsive.” They are now being made available online as part of The Black Vault’s document archive, preserving both the historical reconnaissance records and the additional context surrounding the Pentagon’s Cold War POW/MIA review.

item.dc:creator: John Greenewald

The post CIA Release Reveals Internal Bin Laden Raid Talking Points, Q&A and Declassification Records first appeared on The Black Vault.
item.content:encoded:
A newly obtained Central Intelligence Agency release provides a detailed look at the material prepared inside the U.S. government for the public rollout following the May 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden, including internal talking points, an extensive question-and-answer package, public-affairs guidance and records documenting the expedited declassification of intelligence imagery.

The 35-page responsive record was provided by the CIA in response to a Freedom of Information Act request filed by The Black Vault with the agency in August 2013. In its July 6, 2026, final response, the CIA said it had located the document in its “database of previously-released records” after determining that an earlier FOIA request had sought records on the same subject.

Searches conducted for this article, however, did not locate the complete document in the CIA’s online Electronic Reading Room or elsewhere through conventional web searches. Some portions may therefore be newly accessible online through this release, although that cannot be fully established. What can be established is that this newly obtained package brings together internal records showing how that information was prepared, cleared and organized for public disclosure.

CIA Withholds Records About What Happened to Bin Laden’s Body

The FOIA request contained two separate items. While the CIA released a previously processed record (at least, in part) responsive to the second, it refused to release records responsive to the first.

Item 1 sought:

“All documents pertaining to the capture of Osama Bin Laden’s body, and all documents pertaining to what happened with Bin Laden’s body after his capture — up to the point of his burial into the ocean.”

The request separately sought records concerning meetings about whether the media should be told of bin Laden’s death.

In its July 6, 2026, final response, the CIA said it conducted a review concerning Item 1 and determined that responsive records existed, but that they would not be released:

“With regard to Item 1, after a thorough review of your request, we determined that responsive records, should any exist, would be contained in operational files.”

The CIA cited the CIA Information Act, 50 U.S.C. § 3141, which exempts certain CIA operational files from the search, review, publication and disclosure requirements of FOIA. The agency therefore stated:

“This determination is not subject to an administrative appeal.”

It should be noted that the CIA did not confirm that responsive records concerning the handling of bin Laden’s body exist. Instead, it said that “should any exist,” they would be contained within operational files exempted from ordinary FOIA processing.

As a result, the newly released package does not provide the records specifically requested concerning the handling of bin Laden’s remains through his burial at sea. The CIA instead declined to search or process that portion of the request under the CIA Information Act.

Panetta Sought Rapid Declassification for the Public Rollout

The package begins with a May 1, 2011, memorandum from CIA Director Leon Panetta concerning a request for declassification “in preparation for Counterterrorism Compound Rollout.”

Panetta wrote that materials had been assembled at the president’s request:

“At the President’s request, we have prepared materials for the public roll-out of the 1 May 2011 counterterrorism operation against a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan.”

The memorandum identifies the material prepared for release as three graphics, a document containing talking points for a background briefing, and another containing questions and answers for use during that briefing.

The three graphics were described as a current image of the Abbottabad compound, an imagery-based line drawing, and a comparison showing the compound neighborhood before construction and after it had been built.

Panetta’s memorandum also makes clear that the government was working on an extremely compressed schedule. He requested that the documents be declassified “on an expedited basis” for use by the interagency.

Clapper Authorized Use of Intelligence Imagery

The next record documents another part of that process.

A memorandum to the Director of the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency concerns the “Declassification of Imagery Products.” It bears the signature of then-Director of National Intelligence James Clapper and is dated May 1, 2011.

Clapper authorized:

“the use of these half-meter resolution products, as well as any text or other intelligence information derived from this imagery, in an UNCLASSIFIED manner for the public roll-out.”

The memorandum says Clapper had reviewed the imagery-based products prepared at the request of the White House.

That authorization was followed by the compound imagery itself: a detailed illustration identifying walls, gates, opaque windows and the trash-burning location; a 2011 overhead image; a preconstruction/postconstruction comparison; and an image of the compound in 2005.

Those images are not newly revealed.

The Defense Department distributed the Abbottabad graphics during its May 2, 2011 background briefing. A contemporaneous copy of the Defense Department material identifies the individual files as the Pakistan map, the 2005 Abbottabad compound image, preconstruction and postconstruction imagery, a 2011 image and the compound illustration.

The National Security Archive later collected the material as part of its Zero Dark Thirty File, identifying the imagery as National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency satellite images and the conceptual compound illustration as a Defense Department release. The Defense Intelligence Agency also continues to make the compound illustration publicly available.

Those earlier releases provide the likely public origin for at least the imagery contained in the newly obtained CIA package.

Internal Talking Points Were Explicitly “Written to Be Declassified”

Following the imagery is a nine-page document titled:

“Talking Points for Background Briefing (with USMIL references)”

Immediately underneath is an unusual parenthetical instruction:

“(written to be declassified)”

The document is dated May 1, 2011.

The talking points divide the presentation among the Assistant to the President for Homeland Security and Counterterrorism, the CIA director and the CIA deputy director.

The opening script states:

“As you heard, the President ordered a raid today against an al Qaeda compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan.”

It describes the intelligence operation as the product of years of work and says:

“Our intelligence and military professionals did a superb job. They deserve tremendous credit for serving justice to Osama Bin Laden.”

The proposed CIA director’s portion emphasizes the interagency intelligence effort:

“This military operation was the culmination of years of careful and highly advanced intelligence work.”

It specifically identifies officers from CIA, NGA and NSA as having worked “very hard as a team to analyze and pinpoint this compound.”

The Intelligence Case for the Compound

The proposed remarks for the CIA deputy director go deeper into the intelligence trail that led to Abbottabad.

The talking points state that detainee reporting after September 11 identified individuals who may have provided direct support to bin Laden and Ayman al-Zawahiri, and that one courier drew particular attention.

According to the document:

“Detainees also identified this man as one of the few al Qaeda couriers trusted by Bin Laden.”

The document says intelligence officers eventually identified the courier’s real name and, approximately two years before the raid, identified an area in Pakistan where he and his brother operated. In August 2010, according to the prepared briefing:

“we found their residence — a compound in Abbottabad, a town about 35 miles north of Islamabad.”

The talking points then walk through characteristics that had raised suspicion: the compound’s size, unusually high walls, privacy barriers, lack of telephone or Internet service and the occupants’ practice of burning their trash.

But the prepared language also acknowledged a fundamental uncertainty.

After discussing the intelligence assessments, the document states:

“No other candidate fit the bill as well as Bin Laden.”

It then says the intelligence community’s conclusion was “twofold”: analysts had high confidence that a high-value target was being harbored there, while assessing that there was a “strong probability” that the individual was bin Laden.

An Extensive Q&A Anticipated Difficult Questions

Perhaps the most noteworthy portion of the release is a lengthy, 14-page section titled “Questions and Answers,” also explicitly marked “(written to be declassified).”

It amounts to a prepared government response book covering questions officials expected to face following the raid.

Among them:

“How confident were you that Bin Laden was there?”

The prepared answer distinguished between confidence that the compound contained a high-value terrorist target and confidence that the individual was bin Laden.

Another asks:

“Why didn’t the US trust the Pakistanis enough to share the intelligence with them?”

The prepared response states:

“The United States shared our very sensitive intelligence with no one until this very tightly held in our own government.”

It then says that decision was made to protect intelligence and ensure the operation’s success.

The document also anticipated questions about detainee interrogation.

One asks whether the reporting came from anyone held at a black site or subjected to enhanced interrogation techniques. Another specifically asks whether detainees at Guantanamo provided information leading to bin Laden’s location.

For both, the prepared response declines to discuss the specific sources but says reporting from “a wide variety of sources — independently verified — helped lead us to this location.”

Questions About the Raid — and Answers Officials Were Not Prepared to Give

The Q&A also demonstrates where officials intended to draw the line publicly.

Asked what unit conducted the raid, the prepared answer says only that it was “a small team of highly-skilled operators.”

Asked how many troops were involved:

“I can’t be specific. It was a small team.”

Asked where the operation was launched from:

“For operational reasons, I cannot share that information with you.”

Asked how long U.S. forces were in Pakistan:

“I cannot get into that level of detail with you.”

The document says U.S. forces had left Pakistan after the operation and states that the mission objective, as directed by the president, was:

“To kill or capture Osama Bin Laden.”

Other anticipated questions addressed whether anyone was captured, how bin Laden was identified, what happened to his remains, U.S. casualties and whether similar operations could be conducted in Pakistan in the future.

Officials Prepared for Questions About Why Bin Laden Was Killed

The briefing book specifically anticipated:

“Why kill rather than capture?”

The proposed answer was concise:

“There was a firefight when our team arrived.”

Another question addressed why the president authorized the operation despite not knowing with certainty that bin Laden was inside.

The prepared response acknowledged that uncertainty:

“We couldn’t wait for absolute proof that might never come, nor could we risk the possibility that he might relocate.”

It characterized the decision as one involving risks the president was willing to take.

The document also anticipated questions about whether bin Laden’s death would alter U.S. counterterrorism policy, the search for Ayman al-Zawahiri, relations with Pakistan, Afghanistan policy and the possibility of retaliatory attacks.

Public Affairs Guidance Shows the Intended Government Message

The final substantive section is titled “Public Affairs Guidance for the Interagency,” again followed by:

“(written to be declassified)”

Its “Toplines” present a condensed version of the message agencies were expected to use publicly.

It states that President Obama had authorized “a unilateral raid” against the Abbottabad compound and describes the operation as the culmination of intelligence work led by CIA with support from partners across the Intelligence Community.

The guidance also contains sections headed “Impact of Bin Laden’s Death on al Qaeda,” “On the Intelligence Case,” “On the Operation,” “On US-Pakistan Relations,” and “Possible Retaliation by al Qaeda.”

Much of that information closely parallels what government officials said publicly in the immediate aftermath of the raid.

A May 2, 2011, Defense Department background briefing, for example, discussed the compound’s walls, privacy barriers, burned trash, lack of a conventional profile and approximately $1 million assessed value while presenting the government-released imagery.

The National Security Archive subsequently preserved extensive material concerning the government’s public account of the raid, including White House briefings and the NGA compound imagery.

What the Release Adds

The significance of the CIA release is therefore not that every fact or image inside it is new.

Much of the substantive account of the Abbottabad operation became public immediately after bin Laden’s death, and the imagery included in the CIA file can be traced to the government’s May 2011 public rollout.

What the newly obtained package adds is a more complete view of the internal machinery behind that rollout.

The records document Panetta’s request for expedited declassification, Clapper’s authorization permitting intelligence imagery and information derived from it to be used in an unclassified setting, the proposed division of talking points among senior officials, an extensive list of anticipated questions and prepared answers, and interagency public-affairs guidance.

They also preserve material in its internal form, which includes passages explicitly labeled “written to be declassified”, rather than simply the public statements that ultimately emerged from the briefings.

The document itself was approved for release on August 22, 2017, and the CIA told The Black Vault in 2026 that it located the material among its previously released records, but searches have not located this complete CIA package in the agency’s Electronic Reading Room or elsewhere online, leaving open the possibility that at least portions of the internal package are now becoming readily available online for the first time. That possibility cannot presently be confirmed.

item.content:encoded:
The 1980 presidential campaign between Democratic President Jimmy Carter and Republican challenger Ronald Reagan became the subject of a political controversy after it was revealed that Reagan’s campaign had obtained confidential materials prepared for Carter ahead of their nationally televised debate on October 28, 1980. The materials included briefing and strategy documents intended to help Carter prepare for his encounter with Reagan, which took place one week before the election.

The controversy did not become public until 1983, more than two years after Reagan took office. Congressional investigations examined how Carter campaign documents reached Reagan’s campaign and whether they were improperly used in preparing Reagan for the debate. The matter became widely known as “Debategate.” Reagan campaign officials acknowledged having access to Carter materials, but accounts differed over who obtained them and how they entered the campaign. Investigators examined several possible sources, and the question of precisely how the documents were originally acquired remained unresolved.

The House Subcommittee on Human Resources conducted an investigation and issued a report in 1984. The investigation documented the possession and circulation of Carter campaign material within Reagan’s organization but did not establish a definitive chain showing who initially supplied the material. The FBI also investigated aspects of the controversy, generating records that later became available through the Freedom of Information Act and other government disclosure channels.

The documents collected in this archive relate to those investigations and the broader controversy surrounding the transfer of Carter campaign materials to the Reagan campaign. They provide a documentary record of government efforts to determine what happened, who had access to the material, and whether federal laws had been violated. The historical record established that Carter campaign documents reached Reagan campaign personnel; the unresolved issue was how the material left the Carter operation and initially reached Reagan’s campaign.

item.dc:creator: John Greenewald

The document, titled Inspection Report of the DCI Counterterrorist Center, Directorate of Operations, [...]

The post New CIA Release Reveals More About Counterterrorism Problems Before 9/11 first appeared on The Black Vault.
item.content:encoded:
A new CIA release obtained by The Black Vault has restored significant portions of an August 2001 Inspector General review of the agency’s Counterterrorist Center, adding details that had remained classified when the report was publicly released more than 15 years ago.

The document, titled Inspection Report of the DCI Counterterrorist Center, Directorate of Operations, was completed in August 2001. An earlier version was approved for release to the public on July 26, 2010.

The Black Vault requested a new Mandatory Declassification Review of the report on January 8, 2019. In a July 6, 2026 final response, the CIA said it had completed that re-review and “determined that additional information can be released.” The agency said remaining deletions were being maintained under Executive Order 13526 and statutory protections incorporated through FOIA Exemption (b)(3).

A comparison of the two versions confirms that the new release does contain additional information. Much of it consists of statistics, organizational details and fuller passages that were only partially visible, or completely removed, in the 2010 copy. Numerous operational details, program names, personnel figures and other information remain classified.

New Details on the Center’s Growth

One of the clearest additions appears in the report’s executive summary.

The 2010 version stated that Counterterrorist Center resources had increased over five years, but the actual personnel and budget figures were removed. It also withheld part of the description of the operations that those resources supported.

The newly released version fills in those figures:

“CTC’s resources have steadily increased over the last five years, with personnel growing by 74 percent during that period and the budget more than doubling.”

The report adds that the Center’s resources permitted it to support “operations against terrorists and liaison relationships that DO area divisions otherwise could not fund.”

Those figures provide additional context for the CIA’s counterterrorism buildup before the September 11 attacks.

More of the Pre-9/11 Analytic Problems Are Now Public

Some of the more notable newly released material concerns the pressures facing CIA analysts responsible for terrorism intelligence.

The earlier version disclosed that analysts were concerned about the constant state of crisis and lacked sufficient time for warning and predictive analysis. But a substantial passage immediately following that discussion was withheld. The 2010 copy moved almost directly from the discussion of analysts trying to “get ahead of the target” to a Directorate of Operations response.

The 2026 release now fills in much of that missing section.

According to the newly disclosed text, following the bombings of the U.S. embassies in Africa, CTC management commissioned a review of the Center’s finished intelligence concerning Usama Bin Ladin and possible improvements in analytic tradecraft.

The report states that the earlier study found:

“significant strides in intelligence reporting, analysis, and the application of tradecraft principles”

but nevertheless recommended that management deliberately set aside analysts for research. It also found that an “eruption of reporting, much of it unreliable,” combined with a “dramatic growth in customer taskings,” hindered CTC’s ability to conduct in-depth research on Bin Ladin and his organization.

The Inspector General reported that 18 months later, those conditions persisted and the analytic group remained “largely reactive despite the infusion of more analytic resources.”

Analysts Were Spending Large Amounts of Time Supporting Operations

Other newly available figures provide a clearer picture of how CTC’s analytic resources were being used.

The 2010 version disclosed that the Center’s Assessments and Information Group, or AIG, provided terrorism analysis, but removed several organizational and staffing details.

The new release states that AIG had expanded from two regional branches, one covering the Middle East and another covering the “rest of the world”, to five branches, with increased attention to Bin Ladin’s network and weapons of mass destruction.

Even after that expansion, however, AIG accounted for only “14 percent of staff officers or only 7 percent of the total CTC workforce.”

Another previously withheld figure shows that analysts estimated they devoted between 30 and 50 percent of their time to counterterrorism operations support, including targeting and planning connected with “penetrations, recruitments, renditions, and disruptions.”

Information Overload and Translation Backlogs

The new release also restores substantially more information about a problem that runs through the report: the volume of intelligence coming into the Center.

The newly disclosed executive-summary language says CTC had to cope with “information overload,” sometimes generated by successful operations against terrorist cells. Officers said they attempted to scan and prioritize material for immediate action, but the report noted that operational demands did not allow the Center to exploit everything it collected.

A later section now identifies the CIA’s Language Exploitation Branch as the unit principally responsible for translating clandestinely acquired foreign-language material.

The 2010 release left most of that page blank or reduced it to isolated fragments.

The 2026 version provides considerably more detail. It states that much of the material was poor-quality audio and could contain accented speech, slang or particular dialects. Translators triaged large quantities of information looking for threat indicators, but:

“the translators cannot process all of the information quickly, and several interviewees expressed concern about what they might be missing.”

The report adds that material from some large operations could take “months or longer to process fully.”

New Numbers on Reporting, Staffing and Funding

Several smaller redactions were also removed.

The new version says the percentage of disseminated CTC reports rated “good” or better increased from 44 percent in 1998 to 48 percent in 1999. Those figures were absent from the earlier release.

It also reveals that threat reporting accounted for 12 percent of all CTC reports disseminated in 2000. Senior officials described the rapid dissemination of all threat information as a “zero threshold” approach, while customers sought additional context and analysis.

On personnel, the newly released report says 40 percent of survey respondents believed their work unit lacked sufficient personnel to accomplish its mission.

And in a discussion of funding, the CIA Inspector General reported that the additional costs associated with the millennium counterterrorism surge consumed an estimated 15 percent of CTC’s fiscal year 2000 budget. The extra expenditures occurred during the first quarter, while reserve funds did not arrive until May and supplemental funding followed in August. Interviewees characterized the period as a “rollercoaster” year.

A Fuller Document, But Significant Redactions Remain

The new release does not fundamentally rewrite what was already known from the 2010 document. Large portions of sensitive operational material remain withheld, including program names, specific overseas activities, personnel numbers, operational locations and sections concerning particular counterterrorism programs.

But the comparison shows that the Mandatory Declassification Review did produce meaningful additional disclosure, as the new version provides a more complete contemporary account of the pressures inside the CIA’s Counterterrorist Center immediately before September 11: rapidly expanding resources, analysts pulled heavily into operational support, difficulties conducting long-term research on Bin Ladin, information overload, translation backlogs and staffing concerns.

The post Navy Releases Hundreds of Pages on Cold War-Era “Advanced Naval Vehicles,” Including Nuclear-Powered Aircraft and High-Speed Warship Concepts first appeared on The Black Vault.
item.content:encoded:
A newly completed Freedom of Information Act release from the U.S. Navy provides hundreds of pages of detailed technical, cost and mission analysis from a late-1970s effort to determine what the next generation of naval vehicles might look like, which includes nuclear-powered aircraft designed to remain on station for days, 80-knot surface-effect ships, enormous lighter-than-air vehicles, wing-in-ground-effect craft and unconventional high-speed warships.

The records concern the Advanced Naval Vehicles Concepts Evaluation, or ANVCE, Project, a Navy study begun in 1975 to help shape research and development for the 1980–2000 period. The project ultimately examined nine broad vehicle concepts through more than 200 studies, tests and experiments. Volume 1 states that candidate vehicles were judged against three basic requirements: they had to “be technically feasible,” “have military value,” and “be affordable.”

The Navy released the records September 23, 2026, in response to a FOIA request filed by The Black Vault in September 2023. According to the response, the Navy located Volumes 1, 2 and 3, along with the appendices to Volume 4, consisting of 939 pages in all. The Navy said the Volume 3 appendices and the main Volume 4 report were still being digitized for later review and release, meaning the current production is not yet the complete ANVCE collection.

Portions remain withheld under FOIA Exemption (b)(1), covering information the Navy says remains properly classified concerning “operations and military plans, weapons systems, and operations,” as well as Exemption (b)(6) for personal privacy.

Volume 1 Was Already Public — The Significance Is in the Detailed Volumes

Volume 1, the ANVCE summary, is not newly public. A copy has circulated publicly online for years; a searchable copy remains hosted by the International Hydrofoil Society.

The same appears that it cannot be said about every page of Volumes 2 through 4. Individual ANVCE technical studies and information about the program have long been publicly accessible, including contemporary technical literature, and former ANVCE technical director Peter J. Mantle devoted a chapter of his 2015 book High-Speed Marine Craft to the project.

Per the report, the Navy considered Volume 2 the centerpiece of the project.

A January 7, 1980, Navy promulgation letter included with the newly released records states:

“These results are the most important products from the ANVCE project.”

According to that letter, Volume 2 drew on 165 separate analyses, surveys and experiments consuming 70 percent of the project’s total budget. Nine generic concepts produced 23 “point designs” which included 13 surface vehicles and 10 air vehicles, plus baseline and existing designs used for comparison.

A Navy Study of What Might Come Next

ANVCE grew out of Defense Department concerns over advanced naval vehicle development in the mid-1970s.

According to Volume 1, guidance from the Director of Defense Research and Engineering instructed the Navy to:

“Conduct R&D and studies necessary to evaluate the technical and military potential and costs of other ANV concepts which offer possible alternatives to the SES.”

The study formally examined air-cushion vehicles, hydrofoils, planing craft, surface-effect ships, small-waterplane-area twin-hull ships, air-loiter aircraft, lighter-than-air vehicles, sea-loiter aircraft and wing-in-ground-effect vehicles.

This was not simply an exercise in drawing futuristic vehicles. The Navy developed engineering-level “point designs,” subjected concepts to technical analysis, estimated their acquisition and life-cycle costs, and attempted to determine how their characteristics would matter against a projected future military threat.

Volume 1 describes Volume 2 as the technical feasibility assessment, Volume 3 as the cost analysis, and Volume 4 as the military mission analysis.

And among the concepts examined in detail, one stands out.

A 560-Ton Nuclear-Powered Aircraft Designed to Stay on Station for 15 Days

Volume 2 offers extensive details on the A/L(N) – a nuclear-powered “air loiter” aircraft.

The Navy was examining how to move beyond the endurance limitations of conventional maritime patrol aircraft. Volume 2 states that the project explored technology that might increase airborne loiter time “to at least a day, or perhaps 15 or more days.”

The study considered supercritical wings, laminar-flow control, advanced composite structures, advanced turbofan and turboprop engines, liquid-hydrogen fuel and lightweight nuclear propulsion, or LWNP.

The nuclear design was substantial: 560 tonnes gross weight, an 88-tonne payload, 407-knot cruise speed, 35,000-foot maximum altitude, 1,600-nautical-mile radius of action and 15 days on station, according to Table IV-3 of Volume 2.

The report makes a statement about what nuclear propulsion theoretically offered:

“Other than crew limits, there is no discernible limit to the endurance of the nuclear-powered aircraft.”

ANVCE selected a 15-day configuration as its nuclear point design.

The technical description went considerably beyond simply proposing a “nuclear airplane.” The aircraft used a high-wing, T-tail configuration with a three-deck fuselage. Volume 2 describes its reactor as a helium-cooled, graphite-moderated epithermal reactor with a liquid-metal sodium-potassium, or NaK, secondary loop. Four dual-mode high-bypass-ratio turbofans were mounted beneath the wings.

The report states:

“For safety reasons, JP-5 fuel is used for takeoffs and landings.”

It also says that “much of the element fabrication” was based upon technology developed for NERVA, the U.S. nuclear-rocket program.

There is an important qualification.

ANVCE did not demonstrate that the lightweight nuclear propulsion system actually worked. The report explicitly states that the project did not conduct an in-depth technical feasibility analysis of LWNP. Instead, it assumed such a system could be made technically feasible and then studied how it could be incorporated into an aircraft.

That distinction is critical when describing the design.

Even with that caveat, ANVCE concluded:

“a practical air loiter aircraft with a time on station of a day or, if LWNP is used, 4-15 days is feasible.”

That was a projection based on the technology assumptions available to the study—not evidence that such an aircraft was subsequently constructed or operated.

Nuclear Power Was Also Considered for a High-Speed Surface-Effect Carrier

Nuclear propulsion was not confined to aircraft.

Volume 2 also examined an SES CVN, a nuclear-powered surface-effect ship concept. The idea emerged from a fundamental problem the study identified in high-speed ships: combining very high speed with long endurance required enormous amounts of fuel.

ANVCE first developed a conventionally powered surface-effect carrier design with a gross weight of 11,165 tonnes, approximately 2,040 tonnes of payload, and a maximum sustained speed of 58 knots in Sea State 3.

The report noted that even this design presented formidable engineering challenges, including transmitting approximately 360,000 horsepower to its propulsion and lift systems.

To explore whether nuclear power could overcome the endurance problem, the project developed the SES CVN using the same assumed lightweight nuclear propulsion technology.

Again, the Navy inserted an explicit warning into the report:

“The ANVCE Project did not extensively explore the technology of LWNP; the feasibility of LWNP was assumed.”

The significance of these designs is therefore not that the Navy secretly possessed operational nuclear aircraft or exotic nuclear-powered surface-effect ships. The documents establish something narrower but concrete: Navy engineers incorporated lightweight nuclear propulsion assumptions into detailed feasibility-level naval vehicle designs and then carried those designs into broader cost and mission studies.

Ships Designed for More Than 80 Knots

Surface-effect ships were among the most ambitious high-speed concepts examined.

Volume 2 describes a planned 3,000-tonne-class SES incorporating multiple new technologies into a ship capable of more than 80 knots. But the report is notable for its caution as much as its ambition.

The Navy warned that such a vehicle would be “exploring new performance boundaries” and that “there is risk involved.”

It recommended:

“severely restrict the operating envelope to no more than 50 kt in any sea state until all engineering tests in that portion of the planned operating envelope are complete”

and proposed studying a 50-knot alternative to determine whether the extra speed was worth its cost.

That tension runs throughout ANVCE: extraordinary speed was technically attractive, but the study repeatedly tested whether the military payoff justified the engineering complexity and expense.

Hydrofoils: 70 to 80 Knots

The hydrofoil analysis similarly looked beyond then-current operational speeds.

After operation of a 50-knot PHM-class hydrofoil, the report recommended experimenting with variable-geometry foils that could potentially provide:

“a dash capability of 70-80 kt.”

The Navy believed that such performance should be evaluated under real operating conditions rather than accepted solely from theoretical analysis.

ANVCE also concluded that hydrofoils in the 1,000- to 2,000-tonne class deserved further exploration, while larger 2,000- to 3,000-tonne versions brought greater technical risk and higher costs.

A “Supercritical” Hull for Rough-Water Speed

The records also detail work on an unconventional planing-ship configuration described as a supercritical hull.

Traditional hard-chine planing hulls encountered increasingly severe power and seakeeping limitations as ships grew larger. ANVCE reported that its supercritical configuration offered the possibility of approximately 50-knot operation in rough seas while substantially reducing hull pounding.

Importantly, this was not only theoretical modeling. Volume 2 states:

“Its seakeeping advantages were verified by model tests within the ANVCE Project.”

The report recommended additional development, particularly to determine whether sufficient internal payload volume could be incorporated without losing the hull’s hydrodynamic advantages.

Separate ANVCE technical work on planing craft was already part of the historical public record, including an assessment describing the feasibility of open-ocean planing craft approaching the 1,000-ton range.

Wing-in-Ground-Effect Vehicles That Could Hover

Another major area was the wing-in-ground-effect, or WIG, vehicle—a craft intended to exploit the aerodynamic lift created when a wing operates close to a surface.

The concept studied by ANVCE could blur the distinction between aircraft, ship and hovercraft.

One configuration used pressurized air beneath the wing. Volume 2 states:

“This scheme gives the WIG vehicle a hovering capability, enabling it to operate over land as well as water.”

The same airflow could inflate flexible end plates for rough-water operation. With the skirts retracted, the vehicle could travel at high speed in calmer conditions, while another configuration could temporarily climb out of ground effect.

The Navy did not claim to have solved the WIG problem.

The study identified unresolved questions involving rough-water vulnerability, pitch stability and high-speed maneuverability. It specifically found that the WIG vehicle was “not very maneuverable at high speed” and could need to climb out of ground effect to execute tighter turns.

Its conclusion was continued research, not deployment.

Giant Airships Return to the Drawing Board

ANVCE also reconsidered lighter-than-air vehicles decades after rigid airships such as the Navy’s Akron and Macon.

Two major configurations were examined: fully air-buoyant, or FAB, and semi-air-buoyant, or SAB.

The project analyzed FAB vehicles with payloads between 50,000 and 150,000 pounds, maximum speeds of roughly 80–100 knots and endurance of up to 15 days.

But scale quickly became a problem.

For approximately 50-tonne multimission payloads, Volume 2 found that the fully buoyant vehicle became so large that ground handling and storage were impractical. Gusting winds also produced forces that raised concerns about precision landing.

Despite those limitations, the Navy concluded that smaller airships still had potential for maritime surveillance and recommended studying vehicles with internal volumes of roughly 1 million to 3 million cubic feet for antisubmarine-warfare surveillance.

A semi-buoyant design examined by ANVCE reached a projected dash speed of 150 knots, although the report acknowledged that the underlying aerodynamic-lift technology was insufficiently developed to produce highly reliable designs.

SWATH Ships: Less Spectacular, More Practical

Not every concept was based on extreme speed.

ANVCE viewed the small-waterplane-area twin-hull, or SWATH, ship as a comparatively modest departure from existing ship technology.

Its advantage was stability.

Volume 2 states:

“The steady platform feature of the small SWATH ship provides it with the seakeeping characteristics of a large ship.”

That made SWATH attractive as an escort and as a platform for helicopters and vertical/short-takeoff-and-landing aircraft.

The Navy recommended further design work in approximately the 1,000- to 3,000-tonne range and even proposed investigating towed fuel pods to extend range.

Volume 3: Putting a Price on the Future

Volume 3 is substantially less visually dramatic than the technical evaluation, but it was essential to ANVCE’s purpose.

The Navy attempted to put fundamentally different ships and aircraft onto a common cost basis rather than judging advanced concepts solely by performance.

The volume calculates development, procurement, operating and support expenses across a 15-year life-cycle period, which the study selected because 15 years represented the shortest service life among the advanced vehicles being examined.

The report states:

“Life-cycle costs were derived to provide an estimate of the total cost to develop, procure, and operate each of the point design vehicles over a 15-year period.”

Costs were generally expressed in fiscal-year 1977 dollars.

The analysis covered considerably more than purchase price: development, production, facilities, initial spare parts, repair parts, ordnance, personnel and operating support were incorporated into the methodology.

That cost discipline sometimes undercut the appeal of more exotic concepts. ANVCE’s broader findings repeatedly caution that increasing performance did not automatically produce enough military value to justify the corresponding expense.

Volume 3 ultimately recommended that the Navy develop better standardized cost reporting and continue refining its life-cycle-cost model.

The Release Is Still Incomplete

The September 2026 release is substantial, but it does not close the FOIA case.

The Navy says it found 939 pages comprising Volumes 1, 2 and 3 and the Volume 4 appendices, while the Volume 3 appendices and pats of Volume 4 itself remain under digitization and review.

Volume 4 may prove especially important because the project documentation describes it as the analysis that matched the advanced vehicles against a projected “Circa 2000” threat environment and attempted to identify which platform characteristics actually mattered in combat. Volume 1 says the methodology traced projected threats through potential tactical, weapon and sensor counters to the vehicle attributes that supported those responses. AdvancedNavalVehiclesConceptsEv…

Until that volume and the remaining Volume 3 appendices are released, the record remains incomplete.

What the present release already provides, however, is a detailed look at a Navy trying to answer a difficult question at the end of the 1970s: not merely what kinds of futuristic ships and aircraft could theoretically be designed, but which ones could be engineered, paid for and given a defensible military purpose.

item.content:encoded:
Background

Before the modern era, cryptography was concerned solely with message confidentiality (i.e., encryption)—conversion of messages from a comprehensible form into an incomprehensible one and back again at the other end, rendering it unreadable by interceptors or eavesdroppers without secret knowledge (namely the key needed for decryption of that message).

Encryption attempted to ensure secrecy in communications, such as those of spies, military leaders, and diplomats. In recent decades, the field has expanded beyond confidentiality concerns to include techniques for message integrity checking, sender/receiver identity authentication, digital signatures, interactive proofs and secure computation, among others.

Below, you will find the declassified FBI File that was labeled “Cryptography.”

The file stretches back to the mid to late 1930s! It is an ongoing FOIA request, wherein many documents have not been released yet, and are being reviewed by multiple agencies. I will continue to add the releases, as they become available.

item.dc:creator: John Greenewald

A newly released collection of records from the Pentagon’s All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office provides a substantially more detailed look at the government-sponsored UAP research workshop held outside Washington, D.C., in August 2025, including a working agenda identifying speakers and panelists, previously unreleased correspondence concerning foreign participation, and evidence that AARO was already discussing a follow-on [...]

item.content:encoded:
A newly released collection of records from the Pentagon’s All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office provides a substantially more detailed look at the government-sponsored UAP research workshop held outside Washington, D.C., in August 2025, including a working agenda identifying speakers and panelists, previously unreleased correspondence concerning foreign participation, and evidence that AARO was already discussing a follow-on workshop months before the first event took place.

The records also document a separate Pentagon engagement with representatives of Uruguay’s official UAP investigative organization, including plans for reciprocal mission briefings, discussions about future collaboration, lunch with senior AARO personnel and a private Pentagon tour.

The documents were released to The Black Vault under Freedom of Information Act case 26-F-1773. The request was filed March 17, 2026, one day after DefenseScoop senior reporter Brandi Vincent broke the story of the invitation-only workshop and obtained additional information about it from the Pentagon. Vincent’s original reporting established that approximately 40 government, academic and independent researchers had participated in the AARO-sponsored gathering and detailed its emphasis on integrating narrative UAP data and applying artificial intelligence to large datasets.

The new FOIA release does not fundamentally alter the publicly stated purpose or findings of the workshop. Instead, its significance is in filling in portions of the administrative record that AARO’s public white paper left anonymous or generalized: who delivered some of the presentations, who sat on the panels, where the workshop actually occurred, and how AARO interacted with at least one foreign government UAP organization before the event.

It is not a complete record. AARO identified 89 responsive pages but withheld 19 pages in their entirety under FOIA Exemption (b)(5), which protects certain deliberative government communications. Portions of the other 70 pages were withheld under Exemptions (b)(5) and (b)(6), with the latter protecting personal privacy.

From a Public White Paper to the Records Behind It

AARO publicly released its 2025 UAP Workshop: Narrative Data, Infrastructures, and Analysis paper in February 2026. The official document described an August 5-6, 2025 workshop sponsored by AARO and hosted by Associated Universities, Inc., or AUI, bringing together 40 participants from government, academia and independent research organizations.

The workshop concentrated primarily on an unusually difficult UAP research problem: narrative reports.

Unlike standardized sensor data, witness accounts can originate in military reports, civilian reporting systems, archives, social media and other sources using different terminology, formats and levels of documentation. The workshop considered methods for standardizing those records, connecting databases and using artificial intelligence and machine learning to process large quantities of material.

Some participants had already publicly acknowledged attending. The National UFO Reporting Center announced its participation on August 11, 2025, just days after the meeting, and later identified Chief Technical Officer Christian Stepien as a participant.

The Society for UAP Studies also subsequently disclosed its involvement and identified several participants. Its account said Michael Cifone delivered a presentation titled It’s All About the Evidence and identified Robert Powell of the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies among the speakers.

Those disclosures are important because the workshop was private, but its existence and some of its participants were not secret after it occurred.

The Working Agenda Names Speakers and Panelists

One of the clearest additions is an August 5, 2025, working agenda identifying people whose names and affiliations were omitted from the generic agenda later published in AARO’s white paper.

The newly released agenda identifies the workshop location as Associated Universities Inc., 2650 Park Tower Drive, Suite 700, Vienna, Virginia, across from the Dunn Loring Metro station.

Opening remarks were scheduled from AUI representatives Tim Spuck and Adam Cohen, AARO Director Jon Kosloski, and Gretchen Stahlman of Florida State University’s School of Information.

The keynote, titled “Setting the stage: Importance of good UAP data,” was assigned to Robert Powell of the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies and Kosloski.

The agenda then names Laura Domine, at the time identified as a postdoctoral fellow at the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard University, for the first session.

Domine’s participation fits directly with the workshop’s technical focus. Her published research includes work on the Galileo Project’s multi-sensor systems for collecting scientific observations of aerial phenomena, including an infrared camera array designed to continuously monitor and classify objects in the sky.

The first panel, “Opportunities and challenges with AI,” was to be moderated by Spuck. The working agenda identifies four panelists:

  • Abigail Haddad, identified as a machine-learning engineer;
  • Elliott Hauser, assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information;
  • Duncan McCaskill, identified as formerly with the U.S. Navy Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office;
  • Matthew Szydagis, associate professor of physics at the University at Albany.

The second day included a presentation by Stephen Breuhl of Vanderbilt University Medical Center and another panel titled “Harmonizing qualitative and quantitative perspectives on narrative data.”

That panel was scheduled to include Cifone; Amanda Focke, head of Special Collections at Rice University’s Fondren Library; Ben Gibson, identified as a social/behavioral scientist at RAND Corporation; and NUFORC’s Christian Stepien.

The released agenda provides a more specific picture than AARO’s published workshop paper of the mixture of technical researchers, archivists, academics and established civilian UAP organizations invited into the discussion.

AARO Was Also Engaging Uruguay’s Official UAP Organization

Some of the more substantive new material concerns CRIDOVNI, Uruguay’s official commission for receiving and investigating reports of unidentified aerial phenomena within the Uruguayan Air Force.

Names of the foreign participants are redacted from the FOIA release under Exemption (b)(6), so the documents themselves do not provide a basis for identifying those individuals by name.

In a July 2025 email, an AARO partner-engagement officer told the visitors that AARO would provide hotel accommodations for several nights and proposed a separate August 4 meeting at the Pentagon, the day before the workshop began.

The stated purpose went beyond workshop logistics.

“On 4 August (Monday), would you two be available for a meeting at the Pentagon to provide briefings on our respective work at CRIDOVNI and AARO?”

The AARO official proposed discussing “the types of UAP data our offices analyze, types of analysis we undertake, and ways our offices can collaborate moving forward.”

The Uruguayan correspondent responded affirmatively:

“On August 4, of course, we will be available for a meeting at the Pentagon, it is of special interest to us to be able to establish a further working relationship with the AARO, and to exchange information and experiences.”

The correspondent also accepted an invitation to present CRIDOVNI’s work during the workshop.

Mission Briefings and “Future Collaboration” at the Pentagon

Later correspondence shows the Pentagon visit was approved through the Foreign Visit Request and Pentagon Force Protection Agency visitor systems.

A July 29 email laid out the planned meeting:

“1000-1030 CRIDOVNI Mission Briefing
1030-1100 AARO Mission Briefing
1100-1200 Discussion of Briefings and Future Collaboration”

AARO then planned to host the visitors for lunch and a private Pentagon tour.

AARO also provided a detailed list of what it wanted to learn from CRIDOVNI, including its investigative process, analytical methods and tools, handling of cases containing little or no technical data, notable cases in its database, its organizational relationship with the Uruguayan Air Force, and its scientific and governmental partnerships.

Another email states that a Pentagon lunch reservation had been arranged involving Kosloski and AARO Chief Technology Officer Josh Reiter.

The records do not establish what ultimately resulted from the discussions, whether any formal information-sharing arrangement was reached, or whether the contemplated collaboration continued afterward. No such conclusion can be drawn from the released pages.

They do establish that AARO was actively discussing future cooperation with CRIDOVNI and exchanging information about how the two organizations investigated UAP.

AARO Wanted More South American Participation

The correspondence also provides a glimpse into AARO’s effort to expand participation beyond the United States.

In one email, the AARO official wrote:

“We currently do not have any other registered guests from South America.”

The official said an invitation had been sent through a Chilean contact in Washington in an effort to bring in participants from SEFAA, but that no response had been received.

AARO then asked the Uruguayan representatives for contacts with other South American UAP research organizations that could potentially be invited to a later event.

That request led directly to another notable disclosure.

A Follow-On Workshop Was Already Being Planned

The released email states:

“AARO plans to hold a follow-on data workshop in early 2026, so if you have contact information for other UAP research organizations in South America that you could share with us, we would very much appreciate it and like to extend invitations to them as well.”

The same message described most participants in the 2025 gathering as coming from “U.S.-based universities or UAP research organizations, along with several people from U.S. federal agencies.”

The reference is notable when compared with what the Pentagon publicly said months later.

In Vincent’s March 16 DefenseScoop report, Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough said AARO hoped to convene future workshops and collaborative opportunities “as needed,” but DefenseScoop reported that Gough said AARO had no additional workshops or plans to announce at that time.

The two statements are not necessarily contradictory. The July 2025 email describes an internal plan for a follow-on workshop in early 2026; Gough’s March 2026 statement concerned what AARO had to announce publicly at that point. The released records do not establish whether the contemplated early-2026 event occurred, was postponed, changed form or was canceled.

They do establish that, before the first workshop had even taken place, AARO personnel were already telling prospective partners that another data workshop was planned.

Hospitality Went Beyond the Formal Workshop

The correspondence also shows the degree of personal and logistical attention provided to the Uruguayan visitors.

AARO arranged airport pickup, hotel accommodations and the Pentagon visit. The emails additionally discuss a Sunday Catholic Mass with Kosloski and the visitor and his wife. One message states:

“Perfect, Dr. Kosloski plans to pick you and your wife up from the hotel on August 3 and drive you to mass.”

The same email explains that Kosloski would locate a church near the visitors’ Virginia hotel.

These details do not bear directly on AARO’s UAP analysis, but they document the level of engagement surrounding the foreign delegation and provide context for a relationship that extended beyond simply registering two people for a conference.

Nineteen Pages Withheld Completely

The release also demonstrates the limits of what AARO was willing to disclose through FOIA.

The Black Vault’s request was intentionally broad. It sought attendee and invitation records, agendas, presentations, breakout materials, notes, transcripts, recordings, records concerning destruction of recordings, after-action reports, drafts of the public white paper, correspondence, contracts, funding records, IRB documentation and records concerning future workshops.

AARO reported locating 89 responsive pages.

Nineteen were withheld completely under Exemption (b)(5), with the agency describing them as inter- or intra-agency records that were deliberative and contained “subjective evaluations, opinions and recommendations.” Portions of the remaining 70 pages were withheld under the same exemption and under the personal-privacy provisions of Exemption (b)(6).

Several pages in the released package consist solely of a page number and a (b)(5) withholding notation, providing no indication of the underlying content.

Consequently, the release cannot be treated as a complete reconstruction of the workshop or AARO’s internal deliberations about it.

The Public Paper Went Through Pentagon Review

The records also include the Defense Department’s DD Form 1910 clearance paperwork for the eventual workshop paper.

The form identifies Kosloski as the author and describes the document as an 18-page white paper titled 2025 UAP Workshop: Narrative Data, Infrastructures, and Analysis. It states:

“This 18-page white paper captures findings and outcomes from an unclassified, AUI-hosted, AARO-sponsored interdisciplinary working group focused on narrative and technical UAP data integration.”

The form states that AUI intended to publish the paper on its website while AARO planned to promote it through social media and link to it from AARO.mil.

A More Detailed Picture of AARO’s Outreach

Taken together, the newly released material provides less of a revelation about what the workshop concluded than about how AARO assembled it and what the office was trying to build around it.

The public white paper already disclosed the methodological conclusions: standardize UAP data, preserve historical records, connect disparate databases, use AI cautiously, retain human oversight and develop a continuing interdisciplinary research community.

The FOIA records add names, affiliations and institutional relationships behind that summary. They show AARO putting its director on a keynote with a prominent civilian UAP researcher; bringing machine-learning specialists, physicists, archivists, social scientists and civilian UAP database operators into the same program; engaging Uruguay’s official UAP investigative body separately at the Pentagon; seeking contacts with additional South American organizations; and discussing another data workshop before the first one convened.

At the same time, the records leave significant gaps. AARO withheld 19 pages completely, redacted portions of others, and the released material does not establish the identities of all 40 participants, the full substance of the workshop discussions, the ultimate outcome of the proposed CRIDOVNI collaboration or what happened to the follow-on workshop contemplated for early 2026.

Additional FOIA requests are set to be filed regarding some of the above revelations, and those findings will be posted here at The Black Vault, when available.

item.content:encoded:
The Department of the Navy has released more than 1,300 pages of emails and related records involving former Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence Scott W. Bray, opening a broad window into government communications surrounding unidentified aerial phenomena during a pivotal period in the Pentagon’s modern UAP effort.

The records were obtained by The Black Vault through a Freedom of Information Act request filed on May 24, 2022. The request sought emails sent to, from, copied to or blind-copied to Bray containing terms including “Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,” “UAP,” “UAPTF,” “UFO,” “AATIP,” “AAWSAP” and several related phrases.

More than four years later, the Navy responded on September 23, 2026. According to its response, the search located 1,321 pages of responsive records. The Navy withheld 302 pages in their entirety, while releasing the remaining 1,019 pages with redactions under several FOIA exemptions.

Who Was Scott Bray?

Bray served as Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence and Director of the Naval Intelligence Activity during much of the period covered by the records. His position placed him within a network of Navy, Defense Department and Intelligence Community officials dealing with UAP reporting, briefings, congressional interest and the development of what ultimately became the Navy-led Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force.

One email in the release described the relationship directly, stating that John “Jay” Stratton “leads the UAP Task Force effort for Navy… working directly for Scott Bray, our Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence.”

Bray later became one of the government’s most visible officials on the UAP issue. On May 17, 2022, he appeared with Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security Ronald Moultrie before a House Intelligence subcommittee during a public congressional hearing devoted to UAP. The hearing was followed by a classified session.

The newly released records provide a much larger documentary backdrop to that public role.

A Broad Look Behind the Government’s UAP Effort

The correspondence stretches across years and includes exchanges involving Stratton, Defense Intelligence official Neill Tipton, senior Navy officials, admirals, Pentagon public-affairs personnel and other Defense and Intelligence Community officials.

For example, a March 2020 exchange shows Tipton, who was then identified in his signature block as Director of Defense Intelligence, Collection and Special Programs in OUSD(I&S), telling Bray that he had a document “relevant to our discussion the other day” that he preferred to deliver in hard copy. Other correspondence concerning a planned Senate Select Committee on Intelligence briefing includes Bray, Stratton, Tipton and Rear Adm. Kelly Aeschbach.

Elsewhere, the records show Stratton discussing proposed public language concerning the UAP effort and whether it should be reviewed by Bray before being sent forward. Other email traffic includes Vice Adm. Matthew Kohler, Rear Adm. Charles Brown and Rear Adm. Paula Dunn in communications surrounding the April 2020 public release of the Navy UAP videos.

Those are only examples of the names and subjects contained in the collection. The release includes communications surrounding congressional briefings, public-affairs strategy, the UAP Task Force, the 2021 ODNI UAP assessment, media inquiries, FOIA releases, classification questions, senior-level briefings and the government’s evolving organizational response to UAP.

There are also extensive attachments, forwarded news coverage and discussions of claims being made publicly about UAP. Their inclusion in Bray’s email records does not establish that the Navy or Bray endorsed those claims; in many instances, the records simply document what officials were receiving, discussing or preparing to address.

A Large Record With Significant Gaps

The release should not be viewed as a complete history of Bray’s involvement with UAP or of the UAP Task Force itself. The FOIA request was constructed around specific search terms, and the Navy withheld 302 responsive pages completely. Redactions also appear throughout the pages that were released.

What remains is nevertheless an unusually large collection of contemporaneous correspondence from inside the Navy and Defense Department during the years in which the modern UAP issue was developing into a formal, highly visible government effort.

Given the size of the release and the number of separate subjects contained within it, individual email chains and issues may warrant separate examination. The complete released collection is being made available through The Black Vault for independent review.
