item.content:encoded:
PROMIS has accumulated decades of controversy, competing claims and, at times, confusion over what the name itself actually refers to.

The records released by the National Security Agency provide an important distinction.

The NSA’s PROMIS, or Product Management Information System, was an intelligence-product management database developed during the 1970s. According to records released to The Black Vault under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), the system was designed to organize information associated with intelligence reports and give senior signals intelligence managers a way to search, analyze and manage information about those products.

It should not simply be equated with the better-known Prosecutor’s Management Information System, also called PROMIS, associated with INSLAW, Inc. and the Department of Justice.

That distinction became a central issue when the Justice Department investigated allegations surrounding INSLAW and its software in the 1990s. DOJ ultimately concluded in 1994 that there was no credible evidence that INSLAW’s PROMIS had been improperly distributed elsewhere in the federal government or to foreign governments. A subsequent Court of Federal Claims proceeding also rejected INSLAW’s claims.

Yet NSA did, in fact, have something called PROMIS.

The records obtained by The Black Vault document what it was, and then a FOIA request filed in 2013 to uncover those records produced one final surprise nearly 13 years later.

Two Systems Called PROMIS

The Black Vault’s pursuit began with a passage contained in Justice Department records concerning the INSLAW controversy.

On November 14, 2013, The Black Vault filed a FOIA request with NSA seeking:

“a copy of all records pertaining to the NSA’s use of the computer program PROMIS.”

The request specifically cited a Justice Department account stating that investigators had contacted NSA to determine whether the agency “used or developed any program called PROMIS.” According to that account, NSA explained that it had developed a database in the 1970s using the M204 database system and called it PROMIS, an acronym for Product Related On-line Management Information System.

The NSA records subsequently released provide considerably more detail.

A draft Justice Department report sent to NSA for review in May 1994 recounts interviews with NSA personnel about the issue. The document states:

“the NSA maintains a database known as Product Management Information System, or ‘PROMIS.'”

It explains that “Product” was an NSA term for intelligence reports and that the database contained “abstracts of intelligence reports generated by various parts of the NSA.”

Most importantly, the DOJ account records an explicit distinction between NSA’s database and the software at the center of the INSLAW controversy:

“the NSA ‘PROMIS’ is not a software program, but rather is an application of the M204 database management system.”

One NSA employee interviewed by DOJ said she had participated in the original development of the database during the 1970s. According to the document, it was developed “primarily to allow the accumulation of management information regarding the productivity of various NSA divisions.”

That distinction is important because the Justice Department’s own PROMIS was the Prosecutor’s Management Information System, a case-management system used by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices. DOJ records describe that system as a tool for maintaining and tracking information involving defendants, crimes, charges, court events and witnesses.

The common acronym helped produce decades of confusion, but the NSA records released through this FOIA case document an independently developed intelligence-product management database.

Building PROMIS Inside NSA

The released records trace the NSA system to early 1974.

A January 15, 1974, memorandum titled “SIGINT Management Data Bases” described the underlying management problem. The Deputy Director for Operations wrote that existing management statistics were prepared separately by different production groups and therefore were not available in a form that fully met his needs.

The memorandum called for:

“a system which will cut across Group lines”

and provide management data while allowing officials to respond to Intelligence Community questions.

Another memorandum, dated January 21, 1974, described plans to implement:

“an on-line computer system to provide product-related data needed at the DDO level and outside the agency.”

The document also made clear that security was built into the design requirements. Because some of the information was sensitive, the system would need controls governing both security and access. The memorandum stated that access to data, “either in part or in whole,” would be restricted to those who actually needed it.

A February 12, 1974, memorandum described the existing process the proposed database was intended to improve. The older Offline Coversheet Processing system was characterized as costly and inadequate, with manual data conversion alone consuming approximately 500 man-hours each quarter. Output could lag by roughly two weeks, while the memorandum estimated an error rate of seven to eight percent.

By May 1974, the name PROMIS was explicitly appearing in the records.

A May 8 memorandum titled “PROMIS Content and Timeliness Requirements” discussed a study of the database and asked what SIGINT products should be included initially, what products should eventually be covered and how current the information needed to be.

The memorandum stated:

“We expect to conclude the study and to recommend a system for PROMIS in the very near future.”

The surviving documents therefore portray PROMIS not as a mysterious stand-alone surveillance package, but as a management and retrieval system built around NSA intelligence “products,” with requirements involving searchable information, access controls, timeliness and the handling of sensitive SIGINT data.

The Black Vault’s FOIA Pursuit

Obtaining those records became its own unusually long story.

The Black Vault filed the request on November 14, 2013.

By March 2016, NSA had located a substantial volume of potentially responsive material but sought $440 in fees to continue processing the request. The Black Vault did not pay the requested amount, and there was no expectation that a release would follow.

Then, unexpectedly, one did.

On October 4, 2018, nearly five years after the original request, NSA sent The Black Vault a partial release. The agency wrote:

“Your request has been processed under the FOIA and some of the documents you requested are enclosed.”

NSA withheld portions under FOIA Exemptions 1, 3 and 6, citing classified national-security information, statutory protections applicable to NSA activities and personal privacy.

Significantly, the October 4 letter also stated:

“Additional documents will be provided when their processing is complete.”

The first release included internal NSA memoranda from the 1970s describing the creation and requirements of the system, along with Justice Department correspondence concerning its later INSLAW investigation.

A second, much larger release followed on October 22, 2018. That production contained 85 pages, including a PROMIS user’s manual and additional memoranda. NSA characterized that production as the final release in the case. The Black Vault subsequently archived the material on this page.

And for years, that appeared to be the end of FOIA case 75611.

It wasn’t.

An Unexpected Letter — Nearly Eight Years Later

On April 29, 2026, The Black Vault received another response from NSA.

There had been no indication to The Black Vault that the 2013 request remained open, and nearly eight years had passed since NSA’s October 2018 releases.

Nevertheless, NSA’s new letter identified the same underlying November 14, 2013 request and described the 2026 correspondence as:

“a final response to your Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request”

The agency then provided an explanation for why a case that had seemingly ended years earlier had suddenly produced another record:

“During a review of our files, we located one document that was not provided to you with our final response to your request.”

NSA said it had reviewed the newly located document under FOIA and released it with redactions. Portions were withheld under the statutory protection applicable to NSA, while NSA also stated that the CIA had requested protection of CIA information under FOIA Exemptions 6 and 3.

The newly released record was dated February 8, 1978.

Its subject was:

“Regular PROMIS Listings for CIA”

That document added a significant piece to the historical record.

Addressed to the DDO from NSA’s Chief, V, the memorandum states that an individual identified as being with CIA/COMP had asked NSA to provide “regular quarterly PROMIS listings” for certain sites. Portions identifying the sites remain redacted.

The memorandum indicates that NSA had previously provided the information on a “one-time basis” the preceding August. The author then questioned whether NSA should establish recurring distribution:

“I don’t see any grounds for standing fast on one-time lists, since we are providing monthly listings for [redacted]”

and noted that another party was “obviously aware of this agreement.”

The identities and portions of the operational context remain withheld, preventing a complete reconstruction of what information was being supplied and to whom. The document does, however, establish that by 1978 NSA officials were discussing providing CIA personnel with recurring PROMIS-generated listings and that at least one earlier PROMIS listing had already been supplied.

What the Records Establish — and What They Do Not

The documents now accumulated through this FOIA case establish that NSA developed a system called PROMIS during the 1970s; that the name referred to a product-management database associated with intelligence reporting; that the system grew out of an effort to replace or supplement cumbersome offline management processes; and that its design contemplated searchable product information with controls over sensitive SIGINT data.

They also show that PROMIS information crossed organizational boundaries. The January 1974 planning records contemplated information needed “outside the agency,” while the newly released 1978 memorandum documents discussions about recurring PROMIS listings for CIA.

What these records do not establish is equally important.

They do not demonstrate that NSA’s PROMIS was INSLAW’s Prosecutor’s Management Information System. In fact, the Justice Department material contained within NSA’s own release specifically records NSA personnel distinguishing the agency’s PROMIS database from a separate software program. Nor do the released records, standing alone, substantiate broader claims that have circulated for decades connecting PROMIS to later NSA surveillance systems.

The documentary record supports a narrower conclusion: NSA developed and operated a PROMIS database for managing intelligence-product information beginning in the 1970s, and surviving records show the system being discussed internally and in connection with information provided to the CIA.

The history of the FOIA request has now lasted almost as long as some modern government information systems themselves. A request submitted in November 2013 produced records in 2018, appeared finished, and then resurfaced without warning in April 2026 when NSA discovered that a responsive 1978 document had been left out of its earlier final production.

Whether additional responsive records remain undiscovered is unknown. NSA’s April 29, 2026, letter again labels its response “final.”

For now, the documents below represent the record released by the government, including the document NSA itself found nearly eight years after its previous final response.

Although I did not respond, I was surprised to receive this in October of 2018. It appears that this is only part of what the NSA has on PROMIS, and additional records are still being processed. I will add them when they are released to me.

item.content:encoded:
More than nine years after a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request was submitted to the National Security Agency, the agency has released a heavily redacted copy of a 1972 NSA Technical Journal article titled “Maybe It’s Related to the Phase of the Moon…”

The Black Vault submitted the request on August 6, 2017, seeking the article, which was published in the Fall 1972 edition of the journal. The NSA ultimately processed the request as FOIA Case 102240 and issued its response on August 25, 2026.

The article, written by Herbert S. Guy, Jr., concerns the analysis of a callsign system. The portion released on the opening page describes it as “the story of the dissection of a callsign system” and discusses the overlapping work of cryptanalysts, traffic analysts and linguists.

However, only a relatively small portion of the underlying article is readable in the release. Large sections, including entire pages, remain withheld.

In its response, the NSA stated that the withheld material is exempt under FOIA Exemption 3, which permits withholding information protected from disclosure by another federal statute. According to the agency:

“The specific statute applicable in this case is Section 6, Public Law 86-36 (50 U.S. Code 3605).”

The NSA further stated that it “reasonably foresees that disclosure of the withheld information would be harmful to an interest that is protected by the identified exemption.”

The Black Vault intends to appeal the redactions and seek additional disclosure of the material withheld from the 1972 article. Any subsequent appeal determination or additional release will be added to this archive as the FOIA case progresses.
